| material_system | str | Material studied (e.g., Si1-xGex alloy, SiGeC, SiGe with substitutional C, SiGe with SiC nanoinclusions/precipitates, nanocrystalline SiGe, amorphous SiGe, strained SiGe). Include any explicit formulae as written. |
| sample_or_model_type | str | Whether the study is experimental sample, atomistic simulation model, or first-principles model; include key descriptors (bulk, thin film, superlattice, nanowire, nanocrystalline/polycrystalline, composite with inclusions). |
| alloy_composition | str | Ge fraction x (and any spatial/compositional profile) and other compositional details (e.g., Si0.8Ge0.2). Include uncertainty/range if given. |
| carbon_incorporation_mode | str | How carbon is incorporated: substitutional/interstitial C, C doping level, SiC nanoinclusions/precipitates/nanoparticles, C clustering, or no carbon. Include site information if specified. |
| carbon_content_and_inclusion_stats | str | Quantitative C content (at.%, mol%, fraction) and for SiC inclusions: size/diameter, volume fraction, number density, distribution, interface type, and any stated morphology. Null if not reported. |
| grain_boundary_characteristics | str | Any grain size, grain boundary density, boundary type (e.g., tilt/twist), misorientation, or Kapitza/TBR parameters; also whether model includes explicit GBs or uses effective scattering. Null if not reported. |
| biaxial_strain_state | str | Biaxial strain value (%, tensile/compressive), how applied (epitaxial mismatch, imposed strain in simulation), orientation (e.g., (001)), and whether strain relaxation is discussed. |
| amorphisation_state | str | Whether the system is crystalline, partially amorphous, amorphous; any metric (e.g., radial distribution function evidence, amorphous fraction) and how amorphisation was induced (implantation, melt-quench MD, irradiation). |
| temperature_and_conditions | str | Temperature(s) at which lattice thermal conductivity is reported, plus conditions like pressure, boundary conditions (for simulations), and measurement environment if given. |
| thermal_conductivity_values | str | Reported thermal conductivity with clear identification of lattice component if available (k_L). Include numeric values, units (W/m-K), directionality/anisotropy, and dependence on T, x, grain size, strain, C content, etc. |
| separation_of_lattice_vs_electronic | str | Whether and how the paper separates lattice and electronic thermal conductivity (e.g., Wiedemann–Franz subtraction, direct phonon-only simulation). Include any Lorenz number assumptions if stated. |
| methodology_category | str | Primary approach: experiment (e.g., TDTR, 3-omega), equilibrium MD (Green–Kubo), NEMD, spectral energy density (SED), lattice dynamics/ALD, DFT+phonon BTE, Monte Carlo phonon transport, hybrid/multiscale, etc. |
| interatomic_potential_or_force_model | str | Specific interatomic potential or force model used (e.g., Tersoff parameterization name/year, Stillinger–Weber, MEAM, REBO, GAP, SNAP, MTP, NequIP, DeePMD, qTB). If DFT-based, state functional/pseudopotentials if provided. |
| potential_training_and_validation_details | str | For machine-learned potentials: training dataset composition (structures, compositions, strain states), reference level of theory (DFT settings), validation metrics, and stated domain of applicability. Null if not applicable. |
| phonon_bte_details | str | For DFT-BTE: software (e.g., ShengBTE, phono3py), order of force constants (2nd/3rd), supercell sizes, q-mesh, scattering processes included (Umklapp, isotope, alloy, boundary), and any approximations (RTA vs iterative). |
| alloy_and_defect_scattering_model | str | How alloy disorder and C/SiC/GB scattering are modeled (e.g., mass-disorder Tamura model, virtual crystal approximation, explicit alloy supercells, perturbation theory, Matthiessen’s rule). Include key parameters if reported. |
| strain_effects_on_phonons | str | Any extracted/claimed effects of biaxial strain on phonon dispersion, group velocities, Gruneisen parameters, phonon lifetimes, or mode softening/hardening; include quantitative statements if present. |
| microstructure_mechanisms_claimed | str | Stated physical mechanisms for k_L changes: mass disorder, force-constant disorder, interface scattering, grain-boundary scattering, phonon localization, reduced mean free path, resonance scattering, amorphous-like diffusons, etc. |
| key_comparisons_and_counterexamples | str | Any explicit comparisons (e.g., with vs without carbon; substitutional C vs SiC inclusions; crystalline vs amorphous; strained vs unstrained; Tersoff vs ML vs DFT-BTE) and cases where trends differ from expectations. |
| reported_uncertainties_and_limitations | str | Any uncertainty bars, finite-size effects, convergence notes, known potential deficiencies, or stated limitations (e.g., Tersoff over/underpredicts k, ML potential not transferable, BTE neglects higher-order scattering). |
| figures_or_tables_with_primary_results | str | Pointers to where the main quantitative k_L results are reported (e.g., 'Fig. 3 shows k vs x', 'Table II lists k at 300 K'). Provide identifiers only; do not invent. |

s2_metadata.abstract: We report finite-volume simulations of the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) for heat conduction across the heterogeneous interfaces in SiGe superlattices. The diffuse mismatch model incorporating phonon dispersion and polarization is implemented over a wide range of Knudsen numbers. The results indicate that the thermal conductivity of a Si/Ge superlattice is much lower than that of the constitutive bulk materials for superlattice periods in the submicron regime. We report results for effective thermal conductivity of various material volume fractions and superlattice periods. Details of the nonequilibrium energy exchange between optical and acoustic phonons that originate from the mismatch of phonon spectra in silicon and germanium are delineated for the first time. Conditions are identified for which this effect can produce significantly more thermal resistance than that due to boundary scattering of phonons. [DOI: 10.1115/1.4004429]

s2_metadata.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate the correspondence between first principle calculations and experimental measurements of size effects on thermal transport in SiGe alloys. Transient thermal grating (TTG) is used to measure the effective thermal conductivity. The virtual crystal approximation under the density functional theory (DFT) framework combined with impurity scattering is used to determine the phonon properties for the exact alloy composition of the measured samples. With these properties, classical size effects are calculated for the experimental geometry of reflection mode TTG using the recently-developed variational solution to the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE), which is verified against established Monte Carlo simulations. We find agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements in the reduction of thermal conductivity (as much as $\sim$ 25\% of the bulk value) across grating periods spanning one order of magnitude. This work provides a framework for the tabletop study of size effects on thermal transport.

s2_metadata.abstract: We describe epitaxial Ge/Si multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivities which can be systematically reduced to exceptionally low values, as compared both with bulk and thin-film SiGe alloys of the same average concentration, by simply changing the thicknesses of the constituent layers. Ab initio calculations reveal that partial interdiffusion of Ge into the Si spacers, which naturally results from Ge segregation during growth, plays a determinant role, lowering the thermal conductivity below what could be achieved without interdiffusion (perfect superlattice), or with total interdiffusion (alloy limit). This phenomenon is similar to the one previously observed in alloys with embedded nanoparticles, and it stresses the importance of combining alloy and nanosized scatterers simultaneously to minimize thermal conductivity. Our calculations thus suggest that superlattices with sharp interfaces, which are commonly sought but difficult to realize, are worse than compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers in the search for materials with ultralow thermal conductivities.

s2_metadata.abstract: In our environment, the large availability of wasted heat has motivated the search for methods to harvest heat. As a reliable way to supply energy, SiGe has been used for thermoelectric generators (TEGs) in space missions for decades. Recently, micro-thermoelectric generators (μTEG) have been shown to be a promising way to supply energy for the Internet of Things (IoT) by using daily waste heat. Combining the predominant CMOS compatibility with high electric conductivity and low thermal conductivity performance, Si nanowire and SiGe nanowire have been a candidate for μTEG. This review gives a comprehensive introduction of the Si, SiGe nanowires, and their possibility for μTEG. The basic thermoelectric principles, materials, structures, fabrication, measurements, and applications are discussed in depth.

s2_metadata.abstract: This paper presents a theoretical study of the thermal conductivity of Si–Ge nanograin mixtures using a multiscale computational methodology based on solving the Boltzmann transport equation for phonons with first-principles techniques. A size-dependent correction factor is developed to account for the spatial dependence of the phonon distribution function on nanograin size, with parameters derived from the phonon properties of infinite Si and Ge crystals. This approach makes it possible to accurately calculate the thermal conductivity within a single nanograin, using force constants obtained from first-principles calculations. Thermal energy transport by phonons across grain boundaries is modeled by accounting for phonon transmission by two-phonon processes, weighting specular, and diffuse transmission for each phonon mode as a function of the root-mean-square roughness of the boundary relative to the phonon wavelength. The boundary thermal conductance model, previously validated against experimental data, is implemented using first-principles techniques. This approach excludes specular transmission for phonon modes with specific symmetries while ensuring conservation of the total number of modes in each symmetry class. s2_metadata.abstract: We have used an atomistic {\it ab initio} approach with no adjustable parameters to compute the lattice thermal conductivity of Si$_{0.5}$Ge$_{0.5}$ with a low concentration of embedded Si or Ge nanoparticles of diameters up to 4.4 nm. Through exact Green's function calculation of the nanoparticle scattering rates, we find that embedding Ge nanoparticles in $\text{Si}_{0.5}\text{Ge}_{0.5}$ provides 20% lower thermal conductivities than embedding Si nanoparticles. This contrasts with the Born approximation which predicts an equal amount of reduction for the two cases, irrespective of the sign of the mass difference. Despite these differences, we find that the Born approximation still performs remarkably well, and it permits investigation of larger nanoparticle sizes, up to 60 nm in diameter, not feasible with the exact approach.

s2_metadata.abstract: The ability to precisely control the thermal conductivity (kappa) of a material is fundamental in the development of on-chip heat management or energy conversion applications. Nanostructuring permits a marked reduction of kappa of single-crystalline materials, as recently demonstrated for silicon nanowires. However, silicon-based nanostructured materials with extremely low kappa are not limited to nanowires. By engineering a set of individual phonon-scattering nanodot barriers we have accurately tailored the thermal conductivity of a single-crystalline SiGe material in spatially defined regions as short as approximately 15 nm. Single-barrier thermal resistances between 2 and 4 x 10(-9) m(2) K W(-1) were attained, resulting in a room-temperature kappa down to about 0.9 W m(-1) K(-1), in multilayered structures with as little as five barriers. Such low thermal conductivity is compatible with a totally diffuse mismatch model for the barriers, and it is well below the amorphous limit. The results are in agreement with atomistic Green's function simulations.

s2_metadata.abstract: We theoretically compute the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloy nanowires as a function of nanowire diameter, alloy concentration, and temperature, obtaining a satisfactory quantitative agreement with experimental results. Our results account for the weaker diameter dependence of the thermal conductivity recently observed in Si$_{1-x}$Ge$_x$ nanowires ($x<0.1$), as compared to pure Si nanowires. We also present calculations in the full range of alloy concentrations, $0 \leq x \leq 1$, which may serve as a basis for comparison with future experiments on high alloy concentration nanowires.

s2_metadata.abstract: Nanocrystalline thermoelectric materials based on Si have long been of interest because Si is earth-abundant, inexpensive, and non-toxic. However, a poor understanding of phonon grain boundary scattering and its effect on thermal conductivity has impeded efforts to improve the thermoelectric figure of merit. Here, we report an ab-initio based computational study of thermal transport in nanocrystalline Si-based materials using a variance-reduced Monte Carlo method with the full phonon dispersion and intrinsic lifetimes from first-principles as input. By fitting the transmission profile of grain boundaries, we obtain excellent agreement with experimental thermal conductivity of nanocrystalline Si [Wang et al. Nano Letters 11, 2206 (2011)]. Based on these calculations, we examine phonon transport in nanocrystalline SiGe alloys with ab-initio electron-phonon scattering rates. Our calculations show that low energy phonons still transport substantial amounts of heat in these materials, despite scattering by electron-phonon interactions, due to the high transmission of phonons at grain boundaries, and thus improvements in ZT are still possible by disrupting these modes. This work demonstrates the important insights into phonon transport that can be obtained using ab-initio based Monte Carlo simulations in complex nanostructured materials.

s2_metadata.abstract: Semiconducting alloys, in particular SiGe, have been employed for several decades as high-temperature thermoelectric materials. Devising strategies to reduce their thermal conductivity may provide a substantial improvement in their thermoelectric performance also at lower temperatures. We have carried out an ab initio investigation of the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloys with random and spatially correlated mass disorder employing the Quasi-Harmonic Green-Kubo (QHGK) theory with force constants computed by density functional theory. Leveraging QHGK and the hydrodynamic extrapolation to achieve size convergence, we obtained a detailed understanding of lattice heat conduction in SiGe and demonstrated that colored disorder suppresses thermal transport across the acoustic vibrational spectrum, leading to up to a 4-fold enhancement in the intrinsic thermoelectric figure of merit.

s2_metadata.abstract: Which sizes of nanoparticles embedded in a crystalline solid yield the lowest thermal conductivity? Nanoparticles have long been demonstrated to reduce the thermal conductivity of crystals by scattering phonons, but most previous works assumed the nanoparticles to have a single size. Here, we use optimization methods to show that the best nanoparticle size distribution to scatter the broad thermal phonon spectrum is not a similarly broad distribution but rather several discrete peaks at well-chosen nanoparticle radii. For SiGe, the best size distribution yields a thermal conductivity below that of amorphous silicon. Further, we demonstrate that a simplified distribution yields nearly the same low thermal conductivity and can be readily fabricated. Our work provides important insights into how to manipulate the full spectrum of phonons and will guide the design of more efficient thermoelectric materials.

s2_metadata.abstract: Thermal conductivity of bulk Si0.5 Ge0.5 at room temperature has been calculated using density functional perturbation theory and the phonon Boltzmann transport equation. Within the virtual crystal approximation, second- and third-order interatomic force constants have been calculated to obtain anharmonic phonon scattering terms. An additional scattering term is introduced to account for mass disorder in the alloy. In the same way, mass disorder resulting from n- and p-type dopants with different concentrations has been included, considering doping with III-group elements (p-type) such as B, Al, and Ga, and with V-group elements (n-type) such as N, P, and As. Little effect on the thermal conductivity is observed for all dopants with a concentration below 1021 cm−3. At higher concentration, reduction by up to 50% is instead observed with B-doping in agreement with the highest mass variance. Interestingly, the thermal conductivity even increases with respect to the pristine value for dopants Ga and As. This results from a decrease in the mass variance in the doped alloy, which can be considered a ternary system. Results are compared to the analogous effect on the thermal conductivity in doped Si.

s2_metadata.abstract: Glasses usually represent the lower limit for the thermal conductivity of solids, but a fundamental understanding of lattice heat transport in amorphous materials can provide design rules to beat such a limit. Here we investigate the role of mass disorder in glasses by studying amorphous silicon-germanium alloy (a-${\mathrm{Si}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Ge}}_{x}$) over the full range of atomic concentration from $x=0$ to $x=1$, using molecular dynamics and the quasiharmonic Green-Kubo lattice dynamics formalism. We find that the thermal conductivity of a-${\mathrm{Si}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Ge}}_{x}$ as a function of $x$ exhibits a smoother U shape than in crystalline mass-disordered alloys. The main contribution to the initial drop of thermal conductivity at low Ge concentration stems from the localization of otherwise extended modes that make up the lowest 8% of the population by frequency. Contributions from intermediate frequency modes are decreased more gradually with increasing Ge to reach a broad minimum thermal conductivity between concentrations of Ge from $x=0.25$ to 0.75. Modal analysis unravels the correlations among localization, line broadening, and the contribution to thermal transport of modes within different frequency ranges.

s2_metadata.abstract: Understanding phonon transport in alloys is crucial for the design of high-performance electronic and thermoelectric devices. However, conventional theoretical models fail to provide a clear physical picture of phonon scattering caused by atomic disorder in alloys, and their prediction accuracy is limited. In this work, a new substitutional atomic distance model for alloys is proposed, providing an intuitive physical picture. SiGe and InGaAs alloys are taken as representative systems, and their thermal conductivities are calculated, showing good agreement with previous experimental measurements. The results indicate that alloy scattering plays a dominant role in reducing thermal conductivity. This study provides new insights into phonon transport in alloys and offers guidance for tailoring thermal properties through compositional engineering.

extracted_data.brief_description: Modeling study predicting lattice thermal conductivity (k_L) of crystalline Si containing a fixed volumetric fraction x of Ge mass defects distributed as point defects and variable-radius Ge nanoparticles, using DFT phonon dispersions and an analytic nanoparticle scattering model plus phenomenological grain-boundary scattering; optimization finds discrete nanoparticle radii that minimize k_L and reports quantitative k_L vs Ge concentration and grain size.
extracted_data.citation_title: The best nanoparticle size distribution for minimum thermal conductivity
extracted_data.material_system: Crystalline Si matrix with Ge mass defects (Si1-xGex), where Ge is allocated between point defects (single-atom) and spherical Ge nanoparticles (radii discretized 0.136–5.44 nm); also polycrystalline Si with grain sizes (L) considered.
extracted_data.sample_or_model_type: First-principles-informed phonon transport model (DFT phonon dispersion and relaxation times from ShengBTE/Phonopy/VASP) combined with an analytic nanoparticle-scattering cross-section model and phenomenological grain-boundary scattering; also Debye and Born–von Karman model dispersions used for comparison (all are bulk, isotropic crystal models).
extracted_data.alloy_composition: Ge volumetric fractions x studied include examples: 0.1%, 1% (primary example), 12.2%, 17% (comparison), 33%, 50.8% (maximum discussed); ranges and normalized allocations between point defects and nanoparticles are optimized for each total x.
extracted_data.grain_boundary_characteristics: Grain-boundary scattering modeled phenomenologically via τ_grain^{-1} = v / L with explicit average grain sizes L = 100 nm and 20 nm used in optimizations; no explicit atomistic GB structures, misorientations, or Kapitza resistances reported.
extracted_data.amorphisation_state: Crystalline Si with embedded Ge defects/nanoparticles; amorphous Si only used as a reference conductivity (a-Si k ≈ 1.5 W/mK) — no amorphisation of modeled samples was performed.
extracted_data.temperature_and_conditions: Room temperature (300 K) implied for thermal conductivity comparisons (authors quote k for pure Si at room temperature: 166 W/mK for DFT dispersion, ~150 W/mK for Debye/BvK); transport calculations use bulk isotropic conditions; grain-boundary model uses mean grain size L as boundary condition.
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Multiple reported values (all W/mK): pure Si (DFT dispersion) k = 166 W/mK (room T); For total Ge volumetric fraction x = 1%: alloy (homogeneous point-defect alloy) k_alloy = 86 W/mK (DFT dispersion) vs optimized discrete-nanoparticle distribution k_opt = 30 W/mK. For high-Ge cases: for total Ge x ≈ 50.8% (Fig.2c) best-distribution k_min = 0.89 W/mK; comparison Mingo-style two-size strategy (with alloy matrix plus 0.8% nanoparticle VF) gives k ≈ 2.8 W/mK for a similar total Ge concentration; modified single-size+point-defect strategy yields k ≈ 1.0 W/mK at maximum Ge concentration (50.8%) and k ≈ 1.5 W/mK at x = 33% (≈ amorphous Si value). With grain boundaries: at x = 12.2% and L = 20 nm, k ≈ 2.5 W/mK; comparison without grain boundaries and x = 17% gave k ≈ 2.6 W/mK (quoted for comparison). Directionality: isotropic scalar k reported; dependence: k decreases strongly with increasing optimized allocation to nanoparticles and with decreasing grain size (via the phenomenological τ_grain model).
extracted_data.separation_of_lattice_vs_electronic: Only lattice (phonon) thermal conductivity is considered; electronic contribution not discussed or subtracted (calculations are phonon-BTE/integral based); implicit assumption: phonon-only transport.
extracted_data.methodology_category: DFT-based phonon transport (ShengBTE/Phonopy for dispersion and anharmonic lifetimes) combined with an analytic nanoparticle scattering model (interpolating short- and long-wavelength cross-sections) plus phenomenological grain-boundary scattering and Particle Swarm Optimization to find optimal nanoparticle size distributions. Also comparison calculations using Debye and Born–von Karman model dispersions.
extracted_data.interatomic_potential_or_force_model: Ab initio forces/force constants obtained with VASP; phonon properties and relaxation-time constants computed with Phonopy and ShengBTE. No empirical interatomic potential or ML potential used for transport—nanoparticle scattering modeled analytically rather than via atomistic potentials.
extracted_data.phonon_bte_details: Phonon dispersions and relaxation time constants for the DFT case were computed using ShengBTE and Phonopy from interatomic force constants obtained with VASP (authors cite Jesús Carrete and N. Mingo for these calculations). The paper uses the full phonon dispersion and all phonon modes. Anharmonic (phonon-phonon) scattering lifetimes τ_a were taken from/obtained with ShengBTE; for Debye/BvK cases relaxation constants were taken from ref. 22. The nanoparticle and grain-boundary scattering rates are added using Matthiessen's rule (τ^{-1} = τ_a^{-1} + τ_np^{-1} (+ τ_grain^{-1} if included)). The paper does not explicitly state whether ShengBTE was run in RTA or iterative mode; it reports relaxation-time constants from ShengBTE.
extracted_data.alloy_and_defect_scattering_model: Alloy point defects (individual Ge atoms) are treated using the approach of Garg et al. (mass-defect scattering dominant) — Ge atoms treated as independent point-defects. Nanoparticle scattering rate uses an analytic interpolating model: τ_np^{-1} = v (σ_s^{-1} + σ_l^{-1})^{-1} n, with σ_s = 2πR^2 (short-wavelength/geometric limit) and σ_l = (4/3)π R^3 (Δρ/ρ)^2 (ω R / v)^4 (long-wavelength Rayleigh-like limit), where Δρ is density difference and n is number density of nanoparticles. Matthiessen's rule is used to combine scattering. The model neglects changes in interatomic force constants between Si and SiGe and assumes mass difference is dominant.
extracted_data.strain_effects_on_phonons: No biaxial or other strain effects analyzed; strain is not treated in this work.
extracted_data.microstructure_mechanisms_claimed: Primary mechanisms: mass-difference (mass disorder) scattering from point defects and nanoparticles that reduce phonon lifetimes and mean free paths; geometric scattering from larger nanoparticles (short-wavelength/particle-size scattering) and Rayleigh-like frequency-dependent scattering for long wavelengths; grain boundaries scattering long-MFP phonons (phenomenological τ_grain). Authors assert force-constant changes are negligible compared to mass-difference (citing prior first-principles work). They explain that discrete nanoparticle radii selectively scatter different phonon frequency bands, so a few non-adjacent radii optimize scattering across the broad phonon spectrum.
extracted_data.key_comparisons_and_counterexamples: Comparisons made between Debye, BvK, and full DFT dispersions (all give similar optimal discrete-peak size distributions); comparison to single-size nanoparticle-in-alloy strategy of Mingo et al. (Ref. 9) — best-distribution yields k much lower (factor >3) than Mingo-style; comparison to amorphous Si (a-Si k ≈ 1.5 W/mK) used as benchmark — optimized distributions can achieve k below a-Si for sufficient Ge concentration; grain-boundary inclusion reduces k further for some concentration ranges (e.g., L = 20 nm, x = 12.2% gives k = 2.5 W/mK vs 2.6 W/mK at 17% without grain boundaries). No carbon/substitutional-C or SiC-inclusion cases are considered in this paper.
extracted_data.reported_uncertainties_and_limitations: Authors note approximations and limitations: (1) nanoparticle scattering model is simplified and neglects changes in interatomic force constants between Si and SiGe (justified by prior work claiming mass-difference dominance), (2) the analytic scattering model matches exact scattering calculations to within ~20% (cited), (3) largest nanoparticle size was capped at R = 5.44 nm to avoid complicated intra-particle transport physics, (4) grain-boundary treatment is phenomenological (τ_grain = v/L) and does not include explicit GB atomistics or TBR values, (5) details of ShengBTE calculation settings (q-mesh, supercell sizes, 2nd/3rd order FCs) are not provided in the paper text.
extracted_data.figures_or_tables_with_primary_results: Fig. 1 (optimal nanoparticle size distribution for 1% Ge for Debye/BvK/DFT), Fig. 2 (optimized size distributions for Ge% = 0.1%, 12.2%, 50.8%), Fig. 3 (a: |dk/dx| vs x for several radii; b: nanoparticle scattering rate vs phonon frequency), Fig. 4 (optimal size distributions with grain sizes L = 100 nm and 20 nm for Ge concentrations 12.2% and 50.8%), Fig. 5 (a: k vs total Ge concentration for best distribution, Mingo ref strategy, and modified single-size strategy; b: nanoparticle radius and fraction of Ge in nanoparticles vs total Ge concentration).

extracted_data.name_full: Silicon/Germanium planar superlattice (alternating Si and Ge layers)
extracted_data.brief_description: Frequency- and polarization-resolved predictions of cross-plane lattice thermal transport in Si/Ge planar superlattices using a nongray phonon Boltzmann transport equation with diffuse interface transmissivity; reports effective thermal conductivity vs period length and Si volume fraction and analyzes mode-specific mechanisms (spectral filtering, OP↔AP nonequilibrium).
extracted_data.material_system: Si/Ge planar superlattice (alternating layers of Si and Ge; volume fraction φ = L_Si / L_p varied, period length L_p varied from ~10 nm to >1 μm)
extracted_data.sample_or_model_type: Atomistic-informed continuum/mesoscale simulation model: frequency- and polarization-dependent phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) solved in 1D cross-plane geometry for infinite periodic superlattice unit cell (periodic jump boundary conditions); bulk dispersions assumed for Si and Ge for L_p ≥ ~10 nm.
extracted_data.alloy_composition: Not an alloy; discrete alternating Si and Ge layers. Volume fraction φ varied (examples φ = 0.5 reported); no explicit Si1-xGex random-alloy composition computed in this work.
extracted_data.biaxial_strain_state: Not explicitly modeled. Paper mentions that strain and poor crystal quality in experiments can affect thermal conductivity, but no quantitative biaxial strain or strain-relaxation is included in simulations.
extracted_data.amorphisation_state: Crystalline bulk Si and Ge assumed (bulk dispersions used); interfaces treated as diffuse scatterers (roughness assumed large compared to dominant wavelengths). No amorphisation or amorphous fractions modeled.
extracted_data.temperature_and_conditions: All simulations performed at T_eq = 300 K; infinitesimal temperature gradient (linear response) across unit cell; periodic jump boundary conditions used to represent infinite superlattice.
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Predicted effective cross-plane thermal conductivity depends strongly on period length L_p and Si volume fraction φ: for L_p < 50 nm, k_eff < 10 W/m-K and is essentially a function of period length (interface density) and independent of φ; bulk values used for comparison: k_bulk(Si) ≈ 155 W/m-K, k_bulk(Ge) ≈ 61 W/m-K. At L_p = 1 μm and φ varying, k_eff ranges ≈ 30 W/m-K (φ = 0.2) to ≈ 50 W/m-K (φ = 0.8). Derived interfacial thermal boundary resistance (from nongray results) ≈ 3.3×10^-9 m^2K/W; full-dispersion DMM predicts 2.72×10^-9 m^2K/W; gray model gives 2.09×10^-9 m^2K/W. Gray vs nongray departures exceed 50% at L_p = 1000 nm.
extracted_data.separation_of_lattice_vs_electronic: Lattice (phonon) thermal transport only; electronic contribution not considered (phonon-only BTE). No Wiedemann–Franz separation needed/used.
extracted_data.methodology_category: Nongray phonon Boltzmann transport equation (multiple-band, single-mode relaxation time approximation) solved numerically (finite-volume method) with frequency- and polarization-resolution; diffuse mismatch model (frequency-dependent DMM) for interface transmissivity; comparisons to gray BTE and full-dispersion DMM.
extracted_data.interatomic_potential_or_force_model: Phonon dispersions computed using environment-dependent interatomic potential (EDIP) for Si and the Harrison potential for Ge (used to generate full-dispersion bandstructures that feed into the BTE).
extracted_data.phonon_bte_details: Multiple-band single-mode relaxation-time BTE (RTA) with frequency- and polarization-dependent group velocities and relaxation times; Brillouin zone isotropy assumed; bulk phonon modes used (no confinement corrections for L_p ≥ ~10 nm); numerical solution via finite-volume method with angular discretization (8×8 octant) and 26 coarse frequency bands (derived from 1000-sampled dispersion points along [100]); periodic jump boundary conditions used for infinite superlattice; diffuse (frequency-dependent) DMM used for interface transmissivity; single-mode RTA (energy-exchange via lattice temperature) approximates anharmonic interactions.
extracted_data.alloy_and_defect_scattering_model: Bulk scattering rates composed of impurity (Klemens' mass-defect) scattering τ_im^{-1} = A ω^4 (in paper written as ADp^3 form) and Umklapp scattering τ_u^{-1} = B T ω^2 exp(-C/T) (parameters A, B, C fitted to reproduce bulk thermal conductivity). No explicit alloy-disorder (Si1-xGex) treatment or VCA/Tamura calculations are performed; interface scattering handled via diffuse DMM; no explicit grain-boundary models.
extracted_data.strain_effects_on_phonons: No quantitative calculation of strain effects; text notes that experiments may be masked by strain effects, and other literature indicates lattice mismatch can suppress band-folding signatures, but this study does not compute strain-induced dispersion/lifetime changes.
extracted_data.microstructure_mechanisms_claimed: Primary mechanisms lowering k_L: diffuse interface scattering (interface density), spectral mismatch / selective filtering of modes at Si/Ge interfaces (high-frequency Si optical modes are reflected), resulting nonequilibrium and energy transfer from Si acoustic bands to Ge optical bands that have short mean free paths (extra interfacial resistance), and suppression of long-MFP low-frequency acoustic modes by interfaces. Also: nongray spectral effects increase interface resistance relative to gray estimates.
extracted_data.key_comparisons_and_counterexamples: Compared nongray BTE results to gray BTE and full-dispersion DMM: nongray predicts higher interfacial resistance (~3.3×10^-9 m^2K/W) than gray (~2.09×10^-9) and full-dispersion DMM (~2.72×10^-9). Comparison to experimental data (Lee et al.) shows experiments at 10–30 nm period have lower k than these computations; for very low periods (<10 nm) DMM may underpredict interfacial resistance at epitaxial interfaces. Paper also notes other modeling/MD studies that show minima in k vs period under different conditions and that mixing at interfaces can transition transport from coherent to incoherent regimes.
extracted_data.reported_uncertainties_and_limitations: Limitations stated: assumption of diffuse transmissivity (DMM) and neglect of inelastic/anharmonic effects in transmissivity; usage of single-mode RTA (doesn't explicitly enforce energy/momentum conserving three-phonon scattering); bulk dispersions assumed (valid for L_p > ~10 nm); fitted scattering parameters (A, B, C) reproduce bulk k but MD and first-principles show discrepancies for optical phonon lifetimes; neglects possible partially specular reflections for very long-wavelength phonons; finite discretization details provided (mesh & band discretization convergence discussed).
extracted_data.figures_or_tables_with_primary_results: Fig. 11 (effective thermal conductivity vs superlattice period and volume fraction), Fig. 5 (heat flux vs domain length for single interface), Fig. 9 (temperature profiles across unit cell for different L_p), Fig. 10 (fractional heat flux carried by acoustic/optical modes vs position), Table 1 (description of discrete phonon bands).

extracted_data.name_full: Si0.5Ge0.5 alloy with embedded Si or Ge nanoparticles
extracted_data.brief_description: First-principles (parameter-free) calculation of lattice thermal conductivity of Si0.5Ge0.5 including elastic scattering from substitutional single-atom defects and from embedded spherical Si or Ge nanoparticles, using ab initio phonon properties, an atomistic Green's function T-matrix for nanoparticle scattering, and an iterative solution of the phonon BTE.
extracted_data.citation_title: Role of light and heavy embedded nanoparticles on the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloys
extracted_data.material_system: Si0.5Ge0.5 (Si1-xGex with x = 0.5) matrix with embedded pure Si or pure Ge spherical nanoparticles (nanocomposite)
extracted_data.sample_or_model_type: First-principles atomistic model (bulk composite): virtual-crystal bulk Si0.5Ge0.5 medium with embedded spherical nanoparticles (up to ~4.4 nm treated with full T-matrix; Born approximation used to extend to larger diameters up to 60 nm).
extracted_data.alloy_composition: Si1-xGex with x = 0.5 (Si0.5Ge0.5). Alloy scattering treated via concentration-weighted sum of Si and Ge impurities in the VCA medium.
extracted_data.biaxial_strain_state: No explicit biaxial strain state applied in calculations; strain from lattice mismatch of nanoparticles was estimated to be small and was neglected (authors note a correction term ~ γ (a0 - an)/a0 would be of order that does not change S^2_λ beyond ~0.02 and is therefore neglected).
extracted_data.amorphisation_state: Crystalline (virtual crystal approximation used for the host); no amorphisation studied.
extracted_data.temperature_and_conditions: Calculations reported at 300 K and 800 K (phonon-only lattice thermal conductivity computed); no pressure/boundary-condition details beyond bulk/periodic virtual-crystal medium stated.
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: For bulk Si0.5Ge0.5 (no nanoparticles): κ(300 K) = 10.62 W/m-K (T-matrix scattering rates) and 10.27 W/m-K (Born approximation); κ(800 K) = 6.07 W/m-K (T-matrix) and 6.0 W/m-K (Born). With nanoparticles: relative reductions reported (heavy Ge nanoparticles produce up to ~20% lower κ than Si nanoparticles of same size and concentration); exact κ vs nanoparticle size/fraction plotted in figures (see figures listed). Experimental alloy values cited for comparison: ~7.5–8 W/m-K at 300 K and ~4.5–5 W/m-K at 800 K (authors note calculated values are ~30% higher than experiment).
extracted_data.separation_of_lattice_vs_electronic: Direct phonon-only (lattice) thermal conductivity computed via ab initio phonon BTE; electronic contribution not considered/separated (semiconductor system; lattice κ reported).
extracted_data.methodology_category: DFT-based lattice dynamics + iterative solution of phonon Boltzmann transport equation (first-principles BTE) combined with atomistic Green's function T-matrix calculation for elastic nanoparticle scattering; comparison with Born (perturbative) approximation; virtual crystal approximation for the alloy medium.
extracted_data.interatomic_potential_or_force_model: Ab initio (first-principles) interatomic force constants used; host described by virtual crystal averaging of Si and Ge IFCs and atomic masses. Specific DFT code, functional, pseudopotentials, or numerical parameters are not specified in the text of this paper.
extracted_data.phonon_bte_details: Linearized phonon BTE solved iteratively (exact numerical solution referenced); scattering rates include intrinsic three-phonon processes (Γ^+, Γ^−) and elastic scattering (Γ^0) from alloy disorder and nanoparticles. The Δ_λ coupling term was simplified by neglecting the last term (justified for low-frequency isotropic elastic scattering). Harmonic/anharmonic IFCs obtained from first-principles (references to earlier first-principles phonon-BTE work by authors), but specific supercell sizes, q-meshes, software packages, or order (beyond inclusion of three-phonon processes) are not given here.
extracted_data.alloy_and_defect_scattering_model: Alloy disorder: virtual crystal approximation (VCA) for medium; alloy scattering computed as concentration-weighted sum of scattering probabilities of Si impurity and Ge impurity in the VCA medium. Nanoparticle scattering: exact atomistic T-matrix (Green's function) calculation for elastic scattering by mass perturbation (mass-difference perturbation matrix V); optical theorem used to obtain scattering rates. Born (first-order perturbation) approximation (replacing T by V) also evaluated (Tamura-like limit recovered for single-atom impurities). Force-constant (ICF) differences and strain-related scattering were estimated to be much smaller than mass-difference scattering and therefore neglected.
extracted_data.strain_effects_on_phonons: Authors estimate strain effects from lattice mismatch would add a term ~ γ (a0 - a_n)/a0 to S_λ but evaluate this contribution as small (S^2_λ remains <~0.02) and thus neglected; no explicit calculation of strain-altered dispersions, Grüneisen parameters, or lifetimes presented.
extracted_data.microstructure_mechanisms_claimed: Primary mechanism: mass-disorder (mass-difference) scattering dominates; mass-difference scattering from nanoparticles and alloy disorder strongly reduces κ. Heavy (Ge) nanoparticles scatter low-frequency phonons more strongly than light (Si) nanoparticles — an effect captured by the full T-matrix but not by the Born approximation (Born yields symmetric effect w.r.t. sign of mass change). Force-constant/displacement (ICF) differences and strain are small (~10% or less of total) and not primary. Low-frequency phonons dominate heat transport in the alloy; thus enhanced low-frequency scattering by heavy nanoparticles produces larger κ reduction. Authors use an analogy to potential-well vs barrier scattering to explain asymmetry.
extracted_data.key_comparisons_and_counterexamples: Direct comparison between exact T-matrix and Born approximation: T-matrix and Born give similar alloy κ for Si0.5Ge0.5 (10.62 vs 10.27 W/m-K at 300 K), but T-matrix reveals asymmetry between heavy and light scatterers for nanoparticles (Ge NPs reduce κ up to ~20% more than Si NPs), which Born cannot capture. Size dependence: single-atom impurities well-described by Born at low frequencies; differences appear for nanoparticles ≳1 nm and increase with size; T-matrix calculations limited to ≤4.4 nm (2122 atoms) whereas Born + geometric approximations used up to 60 nm. Comparison to experiment: computed alloy κ higher by ~30% vs experimental literature (authors cite reasons including neglected IFC changes, impurities/defects, and VCA underestimation of scattering).
extracted_data.reported_uncertainties_and_limitations: Limitations explicitly stated: force-constant (ICF) differences and strain were neglected (estimated small but could contribute ~10%); computational limit for full T-matrix around 4.4 nm diameter (2122 atoms) so larger nanoparticle sizes assessed only with Born/geometrical approximations; last term in Δ_λ neglected (justified for low-frequency isotropic elastic scattering); virtual crystal approximation may slightly underestimate alloy scattering (cited recent PRL); no DFT numerical details (pseudopotential, k/q meshes) provided in this paper; authors note calculated κ values are ~30% larger than experiment and discuss multiple possible causes.
extracted_data.figures_or_tables_with_primary_results: Fig. 1 (scattering rates 1/τ normalized by nanoparticle volume fraction for LA branch along (100) for various NP sizes); Fig. 2 (scattering rate 1/τ for 3.3 nm NPs, comparison Born vs atomistic); Fig. 5 (ratio of conductivities for Ge vs Si nanoparticles vs NP diameter) ; main alloy κ values reported in text in Sec. III.

extracted_data.name_full: Si0.934Ge0.066 single-crystal alloy: transient thermal grating experiments and first-principles phonon BTE predictions
extracted_data.brief_description: This work reports reflection-mode transient thermal grating (TTG) measurements of in-plane effective thermal conductivity for a single-crystal Si0.934Ge0.066 (93.4% Si, 6.6% Ge) film together with parameter-free first-principles lattice-thermal-conductivity predictions obtained using DFT-derived harmonic and 3rd-order force constants (SHENG-BTE) within the virtual crystal approximation and additional impurity scattering; predictions are combined with a variational solution to the RTA phonon BTE and validated by Monte Carlo.
extracted_data.material_system: Si1-xGex alloy (specifically Si0.934Ge0.066, single-crystal film on Si wafer)
extracted_data.sample_or_model_type: Experimental sample: single-crystal Si0.934Ge0.066 film (6 μm thick) grown by MOCVD on [100] Si wafer (6° off-cut); First-principles model: crystalline alloy via virtual crystal approximation (VCA) with DFT-derived harmonic and third-order force constants used in phonon BTE (SHENG-BTE); transport modeling: variational solution to the spectral RTA-BTE and Monte Carlo RTA-BTE validation.
extracted_data.alloy_composition: Si0.934Ge0.066 (93.4% Si, 6.6% Ge), single uniform composition reported for the film
extracted_data.grain_boundary_characteristics: Single-crystal epitaxial film (no explicit grain boundaries reported); polycrystalline/GB scattering not included in the study.
extracted_data.biaxial_strain_state: Not reported quantitatively; sample is epitaxial MOCVD-grown 6 μm film on Si [100] wafer with 6° off-cut, but no explicit biaxial strain values or strain-relaxation analysis are provided.
extracted_data.amorphisation_state: Crystalline (single-crystal alloy). No amorphisation reported.
extracted_data.temperature_and_conditions: Room temperature (measurements conducted at ~300 K); experiments in ambient lab conditions; modeling performed for room temperature phonon properties (no pressure variation reported). Optical penetration depth used for modeling: 1500 nm (from ref. [35]).
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Reported as effective in-plane thermal conductivity k_eff versus TTG grating period (1 μm to ~13.5 μm). Paper states reductions of thermal conductivity up to 'as much as fourfold of the bulk value' across grating periods spanning an order of magnitude. Specific accumulated-MFP-derived numbers quoted for interpretation: MFP accumulation at 1 μm gives 0.4 k_bulk = 7.3 W/mK and, by a different heuristic, 0.25 k_bulk = 4.5 W/mK (used to show insufficiency of simple accumulation cutoff). Exact k_eff vs period values are plotted and compared in the paper (see Fig. 6(b) and Fig. 3) but not tabulated numerically in the main text.
extracted_data.separation_of_lattice_vs_electronic: Modeling computes phonon-only (lattice) thermal conductivity from first principles (DFT harmonic + 3rd-order anharmonic + impurity scattering) — i.e., lattice thermal conductivity. The experimental TTG measures total effective thermal transport; no explicit electronic-vs-lattice subtraction procedure (e.g., Wiedemann–Franz) is described, but for lightly doped/crystalline SiGe alloys at room temperature the electronic contribution is implicitly negligible in analysis.
extracted_data.methodology_category: Experiment: reflection-mode transient thermal grating (TTG) for in-plane transport; Theory: DFT-based lattice dynamics (harmonic and 3rd-order force constants) with SHENG-BTE to obtain phonon properties, combined with variational solution to the spectral RTA phonon Boltzmann transport equation; Monte Carlo solution of RTA-BTE used to validate variational approach.
extracted_data.interatomic_potential_or_force_model: First-principles DFT (DFPT / finite-displacement force-constant extraction) to obtain 2nd- and 3rd-order force constants; phonon lifetimes and thermal conductivity computed with SHENG-BTE. Specific exchange-correlation functional, pseudopotentials, or DFT code are not specified in the main text.
extracted_data.phonon_bte_details: Software: SHENG-BTE used for first-principles phonon properties and lattice thermal conductivity; third-order (anharmonic) force constants extracted via finite-displacement/supercell approach (following established procedures of Broido/Esfarjani). Transport solved in the relaxation-time approximation (RTA) for modal lifetimes when integrating thermal conductivity; a variational solution to the spectral RTA-BTE was developed for the reflection-mode TTG geometry and validated against established Monte Carlo RTA-BTE simulations. Scattering processes explicitly included: three-phonon anharmonic scattering (from 3rd-order force constants) and impurity/alloy scattering (mass-disorder/impurity scattering); isotope scattering is discussed in the literature context but not singled out with numerical parameters in main text. Approximations stated: virtual crystal approximation (VCA) for alloy, RTA for BTE (variational trial function uses diffusive Fourier solution).
extracted_data.alloy_and_defect_scattering_model: Alloy disorder modeled using the virtual crystal approximation (VCA) to obtain composition-averaged force constants/harmonic properties, supplemented with impurity (mass-disorder) scattering included in lifetimes (Tamura-like/impurity scattering referenced). The paper outlines VCA approaches (compositionally averaged pseudopotentials or mass-normalized compositional averaging of force constants) following Garg et al. [19] and includes impurity scattering in addition to anharmonic scattering; specific numerical scattering parameters are not tabulated in the main text.
extracted_data.strain_effects_on_phonons: No quantitative study or claims of biaxial/epitaxial strain effects on phonon dispersion, group velocities, Gruneisen parameters, or lifetimes are reported in this paper.
extracted_data.microstructure_mechanisms_claimed: Stated mechanisms for reduced lattice thermal conductivity and size effects: (1) mass-disorder scattering in SiGe scatters short-wavelength (high-frequency) phonons, shifting dominant heat-carrying contributions to longer-wavelength (longer-MFP) phonons; (2) geometric/size effects (grating period comparable to phonon MFPs) suppress contribution of long-MFP phonons and reduce effective in-plane thermal conductivity observed in TTG; (3) optical penetration depth has only weak influence for diffuse-surface reflection TTG in this geometry; (4) fully spectral BTE solutions are required — simple MFP cutoff heuristics or gray suppression functions are insufficient because of the denominator term in the spectral effective-k expression (Eq. 20) that couples modes.
extracted_data.key_comparisons_and_counterexamples: Comparisons made: (a) heuristic thermal-penetration-depth/MFP accumulation cutoff estimates vs gray-suppression-function approaches vs fully spectral RTA-BTE — authors show MFP-cutoff and gray approximations are oversimplifications and can give inconsistent estimates (e.g., accumulation yields 0.4 k_bulk = 7.3 W/mK vs heuristic 0.25 k_bulk = 4.5 W/mK for 1 μm); (b) variational RTA-BTE solution vs Monte Carlo RTA-BTE — good agreement demonstrated for representative limits; (c) parameter-free DFT-BTE predictions (with VCA + impurity scattering) vs TTG experimental measurements — good quantitative agreement across grating periods between ~1 μm and ~13.5 μm. No comparisons involving carbon (substitutional C or SiC inclusions), nanocrystalline or amorphous SiGe, nor explicit strained vs unstrained phonon calculations are presented.
extracted_data.reported_uncertainties_and_limitations: Stated limitations: use of virtual crystal approximation (VCA) for alloy; relaxation-time approximation (RTA) used in BTE (iterative solution not used); choice of variational trial function (Fourier diffusive profile) imposes limitations especially in the q/β << 1 (grating period much larger than optical penetration depth) regime, where the variational approach may fail to capture short-time behavior; uncertainty in optical penetration depth (authors use 1500 nm from ref. [35] and discuss sensitivity in Supplemental Material); lack of specification of DFT functional/pseudopotentials in main text; authors note extension beyond VCA and RTA are left for future work.
extracted_data.figures_or_tables_with_primary_results: Fig. 3 (effective thermal conductivity vs grating period and limits), Fig. 4 (comparison of variational solution to Monte Carlo), Fig. 6(b) (measured effective thermal conductivity vs grating period with variational prediction), Supplemental Material [21] (additional experimental/theoretical details).

extracted_data.name_full: Amorphous silicon-germanium alloy (a-Si_{1-x}Ge_x) — Lundgren, Barbalinardo & Donadio, 2020
extracted_data.brief_description: Atomistic study (molecular dynamics + quasi-harmonic Green–Kubo lattice dynamics) of lattice heat transport in amorphous Si_{1-x}Ge_x across the full composition range (x = 0 → 1), with modal analysis showing mode localization and spectral broadening as primary mechanisms suppressing lattice thermal conductivity.
extracted_data.material_system: Amorphous Si_{1-x}Ge_x (a-Si_{1-x}Ge_x), full range x = 0 to 1
extracted_data.sample_or_model_type: Atomistic simulation models (bulk amorphous glass) generated by melt-quench molecular dynamics; model cell sizes: 1728, 4096 and 13824 atoms (periodic bulk supercells).
extracted_data.alloy_composition: Ge fraction x sampled across 0%–100% (0 ≤ x ≤ 1). Ten variants per composition set; finer sampling near pure a-Si. Examples explicitly reported: x = 0, 0.05, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.5, etc.
extracted_data.amorphisation_state: Fully amorphous (bulk glass). Structures produced by melt-and-quench MD: molten at 4000 K, quenched and annealed (protocol described), final structures at 300 K; radial distribution and angular distribution consistent with a tetrahedral random network.
extracted_data.temperature_and_conditions: Primary results at room temperature / 300 K. MD simulations for Green–Kubo: 10 ns microcanonical (NVE) trajectories with 0.5 fs timestep (GPUMD) for heat flux; model generation used NVT (stochastic velocity rescaling) and NPT (Nose–Hoover) steps; density fixed at 2.32 g/cm^3 for glass generation.
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: a-Si reference k = 2.2 W m^{-1} K^{-1} (room temperature). Alloying: substitution of 5% Ge reduces k by ~0.6 W m^{-1} K^{-1} (to ≈1.6 W m^{-1} K^{-1}); raising Ge to 15% yields an additional ~0.55 W m^{-1} K^{-1} reduction (to ≈1.05 W m^{-1} K^{-1}); maximum reported reduction ~factor of 2 relative to a-Si. Overall k(x) shows a smoother U-shape vs x (shallower than crystalline analogue); contributions split by frequency show the lowest 8% of modes (0–4 THz in a-Si) provide ~half the k in pure a-Si, and these low-frequency contributions are most strongly suppressed by small Ge concentrations. MD (Green–Kubo with cepstral analysis) and QHGK results at 300 K agree within error bars.
extracted_data.separation_of_lattice_vs_electronic: Lattice-only methods (classical equilibrium MD Green–Kubo and QHGK lattice dynamics); phonon-only calculations — no electronic thermal conductivity component or Wiedemann–Franz subtraction needed/used.
extracted_data.methodology_category: Equilibrium molecular dynamics (Green–Kubo) with cepstral analysis; quasi-harmonic Green–Kubo (QHGK) lattice dynamics; anharmonic lattice dynamics (Fermi's Golden Rule) to compute phonon linewidths; modal analyses (participation ratio, diffusivity).
extracted_data.interatomic_potential_or_force_model: Many-body Tersoff potential (Tersoff, 1989) used for all MD and lattice dynamics calculations. In lattice dynamics, the potential was cut off at 2.7 Å (original Tersoff smoothed to zero between 2.7 and 3.1 Å caused numerical errors).
extracted_data.phonon_bte_details: Not a DFT-BTE study. Anharmonic lattice dynamics: second and third derivatives of the Tersoff potential computed by finite differences with atomic displacements of 1e-5 Å; phonon linewidths computed explicitly using Fermi's Golden Rule for 1728- and 4096-atom models; linewidths for 13824-atom model interpolated from a third-order spline fit of the 4096-atom results. QHGK evaluated at 300 K with quantum mechanical heat capacities and phonon populations.
extracted_data.alloy_and_defect_scattering_model: Explicit random substitutional alloying (Si atoms randomly replaced by Ge) in finite supercells; no virtual crystal approximation or Tamura model used. The QHGK generalized lifetimes formally account for mass-difference scattering (no ad hoc scattering terms required).
extracted_data.microstructure_mechanisms_claimed: Primary mechanisms: (1) Mode localization induced by mass disorder (Ge substitution) — localization strongest for low-frequency modes (the lowest ~8% of modes) even at low Ge concentrations; (2) Spectral broadening (linewidth increase, reduced lifetimes) at higher Ge concentrations reduces resonant transport and mode diffusivity; (3) Reduction of generalized velocities (resonant transport efficiency) due to reduced spatial overlap of modes; (4) At low x, k reduction is dominated by localization/reduced generalized velocities rather than a significant reduction in lifetimes (i.e., not ordinary mass-scattering-limited mean free path reduction as in crystals).
extracted_data.key_comparisons_and_counterexamples: QHGK vs equilibrium MD: close quantitative agreement at 300 K. Size dependence: low-frequency contributions (below ~4 THz) show the largest finite-size sensitivity — 1728-atom models differ from converged 13824-atom results mostly in the <4 THz region. Comparison to crystalline Si_{1-x}Ge_x: crystalline alloys display much larger k reductions (up to ~20x) attributed to mass-disorder phonon scattering; in glass, reduction is much smaller (~2x max) and dominated by localization. Literature comparison: Giri et al. (Ref.36) reported up to ~53% reduction in a-SiGe by MD — noted as qualitatively consistent. High-frequency modes become more localized but contribute little to overall k, so their localization has minor impact.
extracted_data.reported_uncertainties_and_limitations: Error bars reported: QHGK error bars are standard deviations over multiple structural models; MD error bars derived from cepstral analysis of heat current (statistical error). Finite-size effects: low-frequency modal contributions require large cells (13824 atoms) for convergence; 1728-atom models adequate for trends but underconverged for low-frequency quantitative contributions. Lattice dynamics required cutting the Tersoff potential at 2.7 Å to avoid numerical errors from the smoothing region — a methodological modification and source of limitation. Authors note QHGK with Tersoff gives excellent agreement with experiments below 600 K (cited), but inherent limitations of classical potential remain. Linewidth interpolation used for the largest model (13824 atoms) introduces approximation.
extracted_data.figures_or_tables_with_primary_results: Fig. 3 shows room-temperature k vs Ge concentration x; Fig. 4 shows k vs x split by frequency ranges (lowest 8%, 8–50%, top 50%); Fig. 2 shows size convergence of cumulative k; Fig. 5 presents modal analysis (cumulative k, DOS, lifetimes, participation ratio) for selected x; Fig. 6 shows correlation between mode diffusivity and participation ratio.

extracted_data.amorphisation_state: Crystalline (mentioned as contrast to amorphous systems).
extracted_data.temperature_and_conditions: Room temperature references implied for reported k values.

extracted_data.name_full: Epitaxial Si matrix with self-assembled Ge nanodot multilayers (experimental HPTR and differential 3ω measurements)
extracted_data.brief_description: Experimental study of cross-plane thermal conductivity of epitaxial Si with vertically stacked Ge nanodot layers (Stranski–Krastanow islands) measured by heterodyne picosecond thermoreflectance (HPTR) and differential 3ω; demonstrates highly diffusive phonon scattering at the nanodot layers giving very low κ down to ~0.9 W/m-K at room temperature for ~15 nm total thickness.
extracted_data.citation_title: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers
extracted_data.material_system: Ge nanodots embedded in a Si matrix (Si with vertically stacked Ge nanodot layers); also comparisons to bulk Si1-xGex alloy (Si0.5Ge0.5 mentioned in simulations).
extracted_data.sample_or_model_type: Experimental samples: epitaxial multilayer thin-film / superlattice-like stacks of coherently strained Ge nanodot layers separated by Si spacer layers (multilayers of 5 and 11 Ge layers; multilayer total thicknesses down to ~15 nm).
extracted_data.alloy_composition: Ge nanodots grown from ≈6 ML Ge for first layer; overall Ge volume fraction in samples < 20% (stated). A bulk Si0.5Ge0.5 alloy thermal conductivity was computed for comparison in simulations (x = 0.5). Exact per-dot composition not specified experimentally.
extracted_data.carbon_incorporation_mode: no carbon reported (no substitutional C, no SiC inclusions).
extracted_data.grain_boundary_characteristics: Samples reported as dislocation-free and coherently strained; extensive TEM and AFM showed no extended defects (no dislocations, pits or mounds) over large areas (e.g., 60×60 μm² for smallest-period samples). No explicit grain boundaries reported.
extracted_data.biaxial_strain_state: Coherently strained Ge/Si islands grown epitaxially on Si(001) (Stranski–Krastanow); strain state described qualitatively as coherent/strained but no quantitative biaxial strain (%) values provided; strain relaxation (misfit dislocations) was checked for and not observed in selected samples.
extracted_data.amorphisation_state: Crystalline (epitaxial) material; explicitly noted to be well below amorphous-limit thermal conductivity and samples are not amorphous. No amorphisation induced or reported.
extracted_data.temperature_and_conditions: Room temperature (measurements reported and discussed at room temperature). Experimental HPTR and differential 3ω performed in ambient laboratory conditions; time-domain HPTR acquisition over 12.5 ns window. No pressure variation reported.
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: Measured cross-plane total thermal conductivity (interpreted as lattice-dominated) down to (0.9 ± 0.1) W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ for a ~15.5 nm thick region (5 nanodot layers separated by 4 Si spacers; period ≈3.7 nm). Interface (single-barrier) thermal resistance ≈ 2.5–4 × 10⁻⁹ m² K W⁻¹ (average barrier resistance ~3.5×10⁻⁹ m²K/W in the 15.5 nm sample). Normalized thermal resistivity per layer ≈ 4.5 m·K·W⁻¹ when normalized by effective Ge layer thickness. Experimental κ values are plotted versus period L in Fig. 2b (and per-interface resistance in Fig. 2a,c). Directionality: cross-plane (through-thickness) only.
extracted_data.separation_of_lattice_vs_electronic: Not explicitly separated in measurements; paper treats reported κ as lattice-dominated (intrinsic semiconductor samples; no explicit Wiedemann–Franz subtraction or electronic contribution estimation is reported).
extracted_data.methodology_category: Experiment: heterodyne picosecond thermoreflectance (HPTR) and differential 3ω (thin-film metal-strip heater/thermometer) to measure cross-plane thermal conductivity and per-interface thermal resistances.
extracted_data.alloy_and_defect_scattering_model: Experimental interpretation uses diffuse mismatch model (DMM) as a limit for totally diffusive barriers; transport picture invoked: ballistic transport across Si spacers with scattering dominated by independent nanodot layers (additive barrier resistances). No explicit alloy-scattering formalism applied to experimental data beyond comparison to DMM and alloy/amorphous limits.
extracted_data.strain_effects_on_phonons: No quantitative extraction of strain effects on phonon dispersion or lifetimes; strain is noted qualitatively (coherent strained islands) but no numerical statements about Grüneisen parameters or phonon mode shifts due to strain are given.
extracted_data.microstructure_mechanisms_claimed: Primary mechanisms: strong phonon scattering at Ge nanodot barrier layers leading to additive interface thermal resistances; barriers behave highly diffusively consistent with DMM (diffuse interface scattering); ballistic phonon transport in Si spacers due to long phonon mean free paths (>100 nm) so that total resistance is sum of independent barrier resistances; roughness/large-size interface features introduced by nanodots increase scattering compared to flat disordered interfaces; no evidence for coherent interference/wave effects (no thermal conductivity minimum observed down to ~3.7 nm period).
extracted_data.key_comparisons_and_counterexamples: Direct comparison between samples with nanodot barriers and literature 'flat' SiGe/Si superlattices: previous flat superlattices report ~3× higher thermal resistance (i.e., higher κ) than DMM; authors' samples reach values close to or below DMM. Comparison of experimental results to DMM limit (solid line in Fig. 2b) shows measured values close to DMM for highly diffusive barriers. Also compared to alloy and amorphous limits (alloy Si0.5Ge0.5 κ computed ≈ 14.5 W/m-K via AGF; amorphous Si limit ~2.5 W/m-K cited) — the multilayers reach κ well below the amorphous Si limit. Contrasted flat-barrier AGF results (higher κ) versus nanodot-barrier AGF results (lower κ).
extracted_data.reported_uncertainties_and_limitations: Experimental uncertainties: HPTR and 3ω uncertainties discussed; error bars provided (HPTR error described in Supplementary Material; 3ω confidence intervals at 68% estimated by Monte Carlo propagation). Limitations noted: experiments on thin stacks (5 and 11 layers) but assumptions about additivity validated by data. The paper rules out dislocation contributions by TEM/AFM. No explicit deconvolution of any possible electronic contribution. Measurements are cross-plane only. No explicit data on dot composition or internal force-constant disorder.
extracted_data.figures_or_tables_with_primary_results: Fig. 2a, Fig. 2b, Fig. 2c, Fig. 2d

extracted_data.name_full: Atomistic Green's function (AGF) simulations of phonon transport through flat SiGe alloy barriers and lens-shaped Ge nanodot barriers in Si (using Tersoff potential and mass-difference approximation)
extracted_data.brief_description: Atomistic Green's function calculations of cross-plane thermal conductivity for model structures: (i) flat Si0.5Ge0.5 barriers (1.63 nm thick) in Si for different periods, and (ii) nanodot-barrier multilayers where 20 nm diameter lens-shaped dots are included via a self-energy approximation; results show nanodot systems give conductivities close to DMM and in reasonable agreement with experiment while flat barriers yield higher κ.
extracted_data.citation_title: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers
extracted_data.material_system: Model: pure Si leads with embedded SiGe barrier regions (random substitution Si→Ge to create local Si1-xGex alloy barrier regions) and model nanodots (lens-shaped, 20 nm diameter, 2 nm height) included via self-energy; also a computed bulk Si0.5Ge0.5 alloy reference.
extracted_data.sample_or_model_type: Atomistic simulation model using atomistic Green's function for multilayer stacks (4 or 10 barriers) with periodic boundary conditions in-plane and semi-infinite Si leads in transport (z) direction; barriers composed of random substitution to mimic alloyed regions; nanodots represented by a self-energy treatment.
extracted_data.alloy_composition: Flat-barrier model: Si0.5Ge0.5 barriers (explicitly stated for bulk alloy computation and for barrier model where random substitution creates 50% Ge barriers 1 nm thick); nanodot barriers: lens-shaped Ge-rich dots with unspecified exact Si/Ge stoichiometry in the self-energy model (referred to as SiₐGeₜ in the paper), overall experimental Ge volume fraction <20% was a target for samples.
extracted_data.grain_boundary_characteristics: No explicit grain boundaries in the AGF model; periodic in-plane and semi-infinite crystalline Si leads (coherent crystalline contacts).
extracted_data.biaxial_strain_state: No explicit imposed strain fields in AGF calculations reported; model treats ideal crystalline Si leads and alloyed regions/dot self-energy but does not report explicit strain or relaxation fields.
extracted_data.amorphisation_state: All crystalline atomic models (no amorphous regions in AGF calculations).
extracted_data.temperature_and_conditions: Simulations compared to room-temperature experimental data (AGF conductivities presented for same context); explicit temperature dependence of AGF not detailed beyond comparison to room-temperature experiments.
extracted_data.thermal_conductivity_values: AGF computed bulk Si0.5Ge0.5 thermal conductivity ≈ 14.5 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (used as reference). AGF conductivities for nanodot-barrier multilayers (4 barriers) are close to the DMM limit and in reasonable agreement with experimental κ (plotted in Fig. 2d). Quantitative AGF values for each period are shown in Fig. 2d (diamonds for nanodot barriers, triangles for flat barriers) but specific numeric values beyond the bulk alloy number are not tabulated in text.
extracted_data.separation_of_lattice_vs_electronic: AGF calculates phonon (lattice) thermal transport only (phonon transmission and MFPs); electronic contributions not part of AGF calculations.
extracted_data.methodology_category: Atomistic Green's function (AGF) phonon-transport simulations with transverse k-grid sampling to include in-plane dispersion and a retarded self-energy to include nanodot modulation.
extracted_data.interatomic_potential_or_force_model: Tersoff interatomic potential for Si (Tersoff 1986) used; Ge atoms treated in the mass-difference approximation (i.e., mass disorder only, no explicit Ge force-constant differences from Si potential).
extracted_data.alloy_and_defect_scattering_model: Barrier alloy regions constructed by random substitution of Si by Ge atoms in 1 nm-thick regions; results averaged over 50 random configurations. Ge mass-difference approximation used (mass disorder only). Nanodot topography (20 nm diameter, 2 nm height lens-shaped dots) included via a mean-field diagonal self-energy applied to atoms belonging to the barrier (to model the modulation due to dots). DMM used as a macroscopic comparison limit.
extracted_data.strain_effects_on_phonons: Not treated/quantified in AGF results; no explicit reporting of strain-induced changes to dispersion or lifetimes in these simulations.
extracted_data.microstructure_mechanisms_claimed: AGF results indicate that larger-scale roughness features introduced by nanodots reduce low-frequency phonon mean free paths relative to flat disordered interfaces, making nanodot systems closer to DMM-limited diffusive scattering; at high frequencies both flat and nanodot barriers show comparable MFPs. Overall mechanism: increased scattering across a wider frequency range due to nanodot-induced interface roughness and mass disorder, reducing κ.
extracted_data.key_comparisons_and_counterexamples: AGF comparison: flat SiGe alloy barriers (triangles in Fig. 2d) give considerably larger κ than nanodot-barrier models (diamonds) demonstrating the effect of dot-induced large-scale roughness. AGF flat-barrier theoretical results are of same order as earlier experimental reports (Ref. [6]). AGF nanodot results are closer to the DMM limit and to the present experimental measurements.
extracted_data.reported_uncertainties_and_limitations: Limitations explicitly noted: Tersoff potential inaccuracies for phonon dispersion (so quantitative agreement not expected to be perfect); Ge treated only by mass-difference approximation (ignores force-constant disorder); small cross-sectional area (1.63×1.63 nm², 72 atoms) due to computational cost limits transverse size sampling, and dot modulation included approximately via a self-energy (mean-field diagonal approximation) rather than explicit large cross-sectional atomic representation; assumption of uncorrelated dot distribution. These approximations may affect quantitative accuracy, particularly for long-wavelength phonons and dispersion details.
extracted_data.figures_or_tables_with_primary_results: Fig. 2d (AGF computed thermal conductivities for 4 barriers: diamonds = nanodot-barriers; triangles = flat barriers) and the bulk Si0.5Ge0.5 reference (value 14.5 W/m-K reported in text).

theory-1.name: Spectral-coverage scattering theory for SiGe-based thermal conductivity (revised)
theory-1.description: Lattice thermal conductivity (kappa_L) in crystalline Si1-xGex and nanostructured Si/Ge composites is governed by how completely the microstructure suppresses the heat-carrying phonon spectrum in both frequency and mean-free-path (MFP). Atomic-scale alloy disorder (mass disorder from random Si/Ge substitution) primarily suppresses higher-frequency (shorter-wavelength) modes and shifts the remaining heat current toward lower-frequency, longer-MFP acoustic modes. Mesoscale features—composition modulation/barriers, nanodots/nanoparticles, and grain boundaries—primarily suppress these low-frequency long-MFP modes via diffuse/interface scattering and/or transmission loss. When at least two scattering classes with complementary spectral selectivity co-exist (e.g., mean composition modulation M(z) + local random fluctuations ΔM; nanodots + alloy disorder; nanoparticles + grain boundaries), the structure can reach kappa values lower than those achievable by either class alone at the same average composition, and can approach diffuse-mismatch-like (DMM-like) limits in cross-plane geometries. The same spectral-coverage lens also predicts when simplistic additivity/Matthiessen reasoning breaks down: when coherence/interference is relevant (very short periods, highly coherent epitaxy) or when the material is amorphous (diffuson/locon transport dominates and the crystal-based spectral partition is less appropriate).
theory-1.theory_query: Build theories of how alloy composition, carbon (substitutional or as SiC nanoinclusions), grain boundaries, biaxial strain, amorphisation and the choice of interatomic potential (Tersoff empirical potential, machine-learned potentials, DFT-based Boltzmann transport) affect the lattice thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex and nanostructured SiGeC semiconductors, based on the following results.
