theory-4.name: Spectral-complementarity scattering theory: broadband κ suppression by combining alloy disorder with mesoscale interfaces/GBs
theory-4.description: In Si1-xGex, alloy (mass-disorder) scattering preferentially damps higher-frequency/shorter-wavelength phonons, shifting heat carriage toward low-frequency long-MFP acoustic modes. To reduce κ further below bulk-alloy values, a second microstructural channel is required that targets these low-frequency modes: grain boundaries with low transmission at mid frequencies, dense barrier layers/nanodots that act diffusively, or optimized nanoparticle distributions that span Rayleigh-to-geometric scattering regimes. The strongest κ suppression occurs when scattering mechanisms are spectrally complementary, producing near-broadband suppression—an effect that can push κ below homogeneous alloy limits and toward (or below) amorphous-like benchmarks in nanostructured crystalline materials.
theory-4.theory_query: Build theories of how alloy composition, carbon (substitutional or as SiC nanoinclusions), grain boundaries, biaxial strain, amorphisation and the choice of interatomic potential (Tersoff empirical potential, machine-learned potentials, DFT-based Boltzmann transport) affect the lattice thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex and nanostructured SiGeC semiconductors, based on the following results.

components.theory_name: Spectral-complementarity scattering theory: broadband κ suppression by combining alloy disorder with mesoscale interfaces/GBs
components.theory_name_plain_language: Lowest κ happens when you scatter both high- and low-frequency phonons with different features
components.theory_description: In Si1-xGex, alloy (mass-disorder) scattering preferentially damps higher-frequency/shorter-wavelength phonons, shifting heat carriage toward low-frequency long-MFP acoustic modes. To reduce κ further below bulk-alloy values, a second microstructural channel is required that targets these low-frequency modes: grain boundaries with low transmission at mid frequencies, dense barrier layers/nanodots that act diffusively, or optimized nanoparticle distributions that span Rayleigh-to-geometric scattering regimes. The strongest κ suppression occurs when scattering mechanisms are spectrally complementary, producing near-broadband suppression—an effect that can push κ below homogeneous alloy limits and toward (or below) amorphous-like benchmarks in nanostructured crystalline materials.
components.theory_description_plain_language: Alloying kills mainly higher-frequency phonons. To cut κ even more, you must also block the long-traveling low-frequency phonons using boundaries, barriers, or the right nanoparticle sizes.

law.statement_name: Alloy scattering shifts dominant heat flow toward low-frequency modes; added interfaces/GBs then become disproportionately effective
law.theory_statement: In Si1-xGex, increasing alloy disorder increases scattering of high-frequency phonons more strongly than low-frequency phonons, so the fractional contribution of low-frequency/long-MFP modes to κ increases. Therefore, microstructures that primarily scatter/transmit-filter low-frequency modes (dense interfaces, grain boundaries with reduced transmission, nanodot barriers) produce a larger marginal reduction in κ in alloys than in pure Si/Ge at the same interface density.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: As you alloy Si with Ge, the remaining heat is carried more by low-frequency phonons—so boundaries and interfaces that block those phonons become especially powerful.
law.domain_scope: Crystalline Si1-xGex bulk, films, and nanostructures at temperatures where phonon transport dominates (e.g., ~300 K), across compositions where alloy scattering is significant (not extremely dilute x→0).
special_cases: At extremely low Ge fractions, κ can be hypersensitive to x and size effects; linearized trends may fail.
If interfaces are highly specular for long wavelengths, low-frequency suppression is weaker than assumed.

supporting_evidence.text: Nanocrystalline SiGe (2% Ge): mass-defect scattering plus GB transmission produces large κ reductions with decreasing grain size, indicating remaining heat flow includes long-MFP modes that GBs can suppress.
Nanocrystalline Si: at 300 K, low-frequency phonons contribute strongly; GB models emphasize transmission near unity at low ω and reduced transmission at higher ω, showing spectral filtering matters.

SiGe nanowire modeling and reviews state alloy scattering suppresses high-frequency phonons, making low-frequency phonons dominate and causing stronger length dependence but weaker diameter/roughness dependence in alloys than in pure Si.

Compositionally modulated SiGe multilayers: combining barrier-like (low-frequency effective) scattering with alloy-like (high-frequency effective) scattering yields κ below both perfect superlattice and homogeneous alloy limits, consistent with complementary spectral targeting.

Ge nanodot multilayers achieve κ close to DMM-like limits; nanodot roughness broadens the scattering influence relative to flat barriers, consistent with enhanced suppression of longer-MFP/low-frequency modes.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Spectral complementarity (alloy for high ω, interfaces/GBs for low ω) is a known design heuristic in thermoelectrics and nanophononics.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: Here it is elevated to a falsifiable law about marginal κ reductions (interfaces become more potent in alloys because alloying shifts heat to low ω) and tied explicitly to the below-alloy-limit observations in compositionally modulated multilayers and nanodot barriers.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Concept is established, but the specific conditional prediction about marginal effectiveness and its integration across these disparate evidence types is a novel synthesis.
references: Wang & Mingo (2010) Diameter dependence of SiGe nanowire thermal conductivity [alloy vs boundary scattering interplay]
Yang & Dames / Minnich-era spectral suppression-function literature [general spectral targeting concept]
Compositionally modulated SiGe multilayers paper [explicit barrier+alloy complementarity in first-principles BTE]

law.statement_name: Broadband design rule: combining M(z) barriers with ΔM randomness (or multi-scale inclusions) can undercut homogeneous-alloy κ
law.theory_statement: For a fixed mean composition, adding a spatially varying mean profile M(z) (barriers, grading, dot layers) while retaining local randomness ΔM (alloy disorder) increases the integrated scattering phase space across phonon frequencies compared with either mechanism alone; thus κ(M(z)+ΔM) can be less than min[κ(homogeneous alloy), κ(perfect sharp superlattice/barriers)] when interface scattering is sufficiently diffuse/incoherent and periods are in the regime where resistances add approximately.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: If you mix ‘barrier-like’ structure with ‘alloy-like’ randomness, you can scatter a wider range of phonons and get κ even lower than a plain alloy.
law.domain_scope: Crystalline SiGe multilayers/nanostructures at room temperature where (i) transport across barriers is incoherent/diffusive enough for additivity, and (ii) both mean-profile and random-alloy disorder exist (interdiffusion/segregation or engineered grading).
special_cases: In strongly coherent superlattices, wave interference can dominate and violate simple additivity; the law targets the diffusive/incoherent regime evidenced by nanodot barriers.
If M(z) is too smooth (adiabatic), low-frequency reflection/scattering can be weak, reducing the benefit.

supporting_evidence.text: Compositionally modulated multilayers paper explicitly decomposes scattering into mean mass-density profile M(z) (barrier scattering) plus random ΔM (alloy scattering) and reports that combined presence can lower κ below both homogeneous alloy and ideal sharp-interface superlattice limits.

Experimental Ge nanodot multilayers show additive barrier resistances and κ near DMM-like limits, consistent with an incoherent/diffusive regime where adding structured barriers reduces κ beyond what flat alloy barriers achieve.

AGF simulations comparing flat SiGe barriers vs nanodot barriers show nanodot systems yield lower κ and are closer to DMM than flat barriers, supporting that adding mesoscale morphology (a form of M(z) complexity) increases scattering breadth.
MD on compositionally graded SiGe nanowires reports substantially reduced κ versus abrupt interfaces (review cites ~57% reduction), consistent with broadened scattering from grading + disorder.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Barrier+alloy complementarity is discussed in the multilayers literature; graded profiles and nanodots are known to impede κ.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: This law states an explicit inequality-style design criterion—κ can undercut both homogeneous-alloy and ideal-barrier limits when additivity holds—generalizing across planar graded multilayers and nanodot barriers as a unifying broadband-scattering principle.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Grounded in existing mechanisms but framed as a portable predictive rule that can be applied to new SiGeC architectures (e.g., SiC inclusions + alloy disorder + GBs).
references: Compositionally modulated SiGe multilayers paper [explicit M(z)+ΔM framework; below-alloy-limit κ]
Minnich et al. nanodot barrier experiments [diffusive/additive barrier resistance; near-DMM κ]
Zhang et al. (2017) graded SiGe nanowires [graded vs abrupt κ reduction]

new_predictions_likely: For Si0.8Ge0.2, introducing nanodot/nanoparticle layers (or GBs) will reduce κ more than the same interface density in pure Si because alloying shifts heat carriage toward long-MFP low-frequency modes that interfaces can filter.

A compositionally graded profile with residual random alloy disorder will yield lower κ than either (i) a fully homogeneous alloy of the same mean x or (ii) a perfectly abrupt, perfectly periodic superlattice of the same mean x, provided interfaces are sufficiently diffuse/incoherent.
Adding a second length scale (e.g., nanoparticles + grain boundaries) will produce a super-additive reduction relative to adding either alone if the two target different parts of the phonon spectrum.
new_predictions_unknown: In SiGeC, an engineered tri-modal spectrum of scatterers (substitutional C + SiC precipitates + nanoscale GBs) could push κ below amorphous-Si benchmarks while retaining crystallinity, if stiffness-disorder scattering from SiC is as broadband as hypothesized.

There may exist an optimal correlated arrangement (not random) of graded composition + nanodots that maximizes broadband suppression without invoking coherent interference, potentially outperforming purely random microstructures.
negative_experiments: If a controlled experiment/simulation shows that adding interfaces/barriers to an alloy reduces κ by the same fraction as in pure Si (after matching interface density and roughness), the predicted alloy-amplified marginal effect is false.
If graded profiles consistently show higher κ than abrupt interfaces at the same mean composition and defect density in the incoherent regime, the broadband-scattering/inequality rule is falsified.

unaccounted_for.text: This theory does not directly address the detailed potential-dependence or endpoint-composition anomalies that can arise in empirical MD fits; it focuses on physical spectral complementarity rather than numerical artifacts.

special_cases: Highly coherent superlattices where wave effects dominate (outside the diffusive/additive regime).
Extremely dilute alloys (x→0) where κ is hypersensitive to tiny x changes and extrinsic defect populations can dominate.

references: Wang & Mingo (2010) Diameter dependence of SiGe nanowire thermal conductivity [alloy vs boundary scattering interplay; spectral shift toward low-frequency modes]
Compositionally-modulated SiGe multilayers (year not provided in evidence) [M(z)+ΔM scattering complementarity; κ below alloy limit]
Minnich et al. (nanodot barrier experiments) [diffusive barrier scattering approaching DMM]
existing_theory.what_already_exists: The idea that different microstructural features target different phonon frequencies and that combining them can reduce κ more than any one feature alone is well established.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: A unified, inequality-style broadband design rule connecting the multilayer M(z)+ΔM formalism, nanodot-barrier DMM-like behavior, and nanocrystalline filtering into a single predictive principle intended for extrapolation to SiGeC architectures.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: Mostly built from existing spectral-scattering concepts but expressed as a more general and testable design rule across multiple SiGe nanostructure classes.

components.mission_statement:
The theories will be used to answer the following questions before the corresponding simulation results are seen. Address the mechanisms they depend on:

H1. Two 3C-SiC spheres of radius R are embedded in Si0.8Ge0.2 (Tersoff MD,
300 K, reverse NEMD). A continuum scattering model brackets the particle's
effect on lattice thermal conductivity between a density-contrast-only lower
bound and a stiffness-contrast-only upper bound. At R = 2.0 nm the bracket is
a 40 % to 75 % reduction of kappa relative to the same alloy without the
particle (with the surrounding composition held equal).
Category for the MD result at R = 2.0 nm: "below", "inside", "above".
Value: the MD reduction in percent.
H1b. In the same set-up, carbon prefers Si neighbours, so the control runs
place each particle inside a Si-rich (Ge-free) shell about 7 A thick. Does a
run with particle plus Si-rich shell conduct heat better or worse than the
bare Si0.8Ge0.2 alloy with neither?
Category: "higher", "lower". Value: percent change of kappa relative to the
bare alloy, for R = 2.0 nm.
H2. A symbolic law for Tersoff-MD kappa of Si1-xGex, of the form
kappa = 1/(a + b x + c x^2 + d T), was fitted on 0.05 <= x <= 0.93 at
finite box size. Points at x > 0.93 sit well above the law and an outlier
detector flagged two of them as isolated faults. At x = 0.90, 300 K, the
same box gives kappa = 4.5 W/mK.
Category: "fault" (the high points are errors), "physics" (they are real).
Value: kappa at x = 0.97, 300 K in the same box, W/mK.
H3. almaBTE (virtual crystal, DFT force constants, full iterative BTE)
gives kappa of bulk Si1-xGex in W/mK:

| x | 300 K | 700 K | 1100 K |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 160.5 | 63.8 | 40.5 |
| 0.15 | 8.33 | 6.69 | 5.72 |
| 0.2 | 7.27 | 5.89 | 5.07 |
| 0.5 | 6.49 | 5.08 | 4.30 |
| 0.85 | 11.54 | 7.83 | 6.21 |
| 1 | 57.1 | 25.7 | 16.7 |

Value: almaBTE kappa at x = 0.7, 1100 K (W/mK). Category: where is the
composition of minimum kappa at 1100 K: "x<0.4", "0.4<=x<=0.6", "x>0.6".
H4. Amorphous Si0.5Ge0.5 is made by melt-quenching with the Tersoff
potential and kappa is computed by reverse NEMD in boxes of three lengths
(24, 48 and 96 conventional cells along the heat-flow direction, 4 x 4
cells across). Crystalline alloy kappa in these boxes rises with length.
Category: "size-independent", "rises with length", "falls with length".
Value: ratio kappa(96 cells)/kappa(24 cells).
H5. Pure crystalline Si: Tersoff-1989 GPUMD homogeneous NEMD kappa versus
almaBTE (160.5 W/mK at 300 K, 40.5 W/mK at 1100 K).
Value: ratio Tersoff/almaBTE at 300 K. Category for 1100 K:
"agree within 30 %", "Tersoff higher by more than 30 %",
"Tersoff lower by more than 30 %".
H6. Ball-milled and sintered Si0.8Ge0.2 with 1 at% carbon. MACE-MP-0
energies compare a substitutional C atom in the alloy with the same C atom
moved into a SiC precipitate.
Category: "SiC precipitate favoured", "substitutional favoured".
Value: energy gained per C atom by forming SiC, eV (positive = SiC
favoured). Also give, inside "theory", whether C prefers Si or Ge
neighbours and by how much (eV).
H7. A Si0.5Ge0.5 film is grown coherently on Si(001) (biaxial in-plane
compression of about 2 %) and kappa is computed by Tersoff MD in-plane and
across the film, compared with relaxed bulk Si0.5Ge0.5.
Category for the cross-plane change at 300 K: "increase", "decrease",
"no change within 5 %". Value: cross-plane change at 300 K in percent.
State in "theory" what happens in-plane.
H8. Starrydata2 holds digitized kappa of sintered (hot-pressed or spark
plasma sintered) Si0.8Ge0.2, many papers. almaBTE perfect-crystal kappa at
x = 0.2, 300 K is 7.27 W/mK.
Value: median ratio of sintered lattice kappa to the almaBTE value at
300 K. Category: "below 0.7", "0.7 to 0.9", "above 0.9".
O3. If the carbon-location calculation of H6 is repeated with a newer
foundation potential trained on more data (for example a MACE model trained
on MPtrj plus Alexandria), does the sign of the SiC-precipitation energy
hold? Category: "sign holds, magnitude within 0.3 eV", "sign holds,
magnitude changes by more than 0.3 eV", "sign flips". Value: predicted
energy gained per C atom, eV.

theory-5.name: Amorphous SiGe localization threshold theory (low-x Ge strongly suppresses low-frequency carriers)
theory-5.description: In amorphous a-Si1-xGex near room temperature, lattice thermal conductivity is governed primarily by (i) how extended the low-frequency vibrational eigenmodes are (propagon-like, weakly scattered modes) and (ii) how efficiently modes exchange energy (diffuson-like transport). Small Ge substitution disproportionately suppresses the lowest-frequency extended modes that carry a large fraction of heat in a-Si, mainly through disorder-induced localization and reduced generalized velocities/spatial overlap rather than a large initial change in lifetimes. At higher Ge content, additional reductions increasingly come from spectral broadening/linewidth growth and reduced diffusivity across a wider band, yielding diminishing returns. In MD/QHGK-type calculations, finite-size artifacts primarily reflect poor resolution of these lowest-frequency contributions; thus the apparent size dependence is a diagnostic for whether the low-frequency sector is converged.
theory-5.theory_query: Build theories of how alloy composition, carbon (substitutional or as SiC nanoinclusions), grain boundaries, biaxial strain, amorphisation and the choice of interatomic potential (Tersoff empirical potential, machine-learned potentials, DFT-based Boltzmann transport) affect the lattice thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex and nanostructured SiGeC semiconductors, based on the following results.

components.theory_name: Amorphous SiGe localization threshold theory (low-x Ge strongly suppresses low-frequency carriers)
components.theory_name_plain_language: In amorphous SiGe, small Ge amounts mainly kill the lowest-frequency heat carriers
components.theory_description: In amorphous a-Si1-xGex near room temperature, lattice thermal conductivity is governed primarily by (i) how extended the low-frequency vibrational eigenmodes are (propagon-like, weakly scattered modes) and (ii) how efficiently modes exchange energy (diffuson-like transport). Small Ge substitution disproportionately suppresses the lowest-frequency extended modes that carry a large fraction of heat in a-Si, mainly through disorder-induced localization and reduced generalized velocities/spatial overlap rather than a large initial change in lifetimes. At higher Ge content, additional reductions increasingly come from spectral broadening/linewidth growth and reduced diffusivity across a wider band, yielding diminishing returns. In MD/QHGK-type calculations, finite-size artifacts primarily reflect poor resolution of these lowest-frequency contributions; thus the apparent size dependence is a diagnostic for whether the low-frequency sector is converged.
components.theory_description_plain_language: For amorphous SiGe, a little Ge quickly localizes (or otherwise de-extends) the vibrations that carry most heat. After that, adding more Ge helps less. Small simulation cells mainly fail by not representing these lowest-frequency contributions well.

law.statement_name: Early-drop law: low-x Ge suppresses low-frequency heat-carrying modes in a-Si
law.theory_statement: In fully amorphous Si1-xGex near 300 K produced by melt-quench protocols, the initial conductivity decrement dκ/dx at low Ge fraction x is dominated by suppression of the lowest-frequency extended modes (the lowest ~few THz / lowest ~O(10%) of modes) via increased mode localization and reduced generalized velocities (reduced spatial overlap), while the mode-lifetime reduction plays a secondary role at low x. As x increases beyond the low-x regime, further κ reduction is increasingly controlled by spectral broadening/linewidth growth and reduced mode diffusivities over a broader frequency range, producing diminishing marginal reductions in κ with x.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: Adding a few percent Ge to amorphous Si knocks out the most important low-frequency heat carriers first; later Ge additions reduce heat flow more slowly and via broader-band damping.
law.domain_scope: Bulk-like, fully amorphous a-Si1-xGex (no nanocrystalline grains) generated by melt-quench MD (tetrahedral continuous random network) and evaluated at ~300 K; applies to lattice-only heat transport described by MD Green–Kubo / QHGK formalisms where transport occurs via propagons/diffusons rather than crystal phonons.
special_cases: At sufficiently low temperatures (well below room temperature), where only the very lowest-frequency excitations contribute, κ(x) may become even more sensitive to small x than described here (not directly evidenced in the provided dataset).

If the amorphous network has substantial coordination defects/voids or phase separation beyond random substitution, the partition between (localization/reduced generalized velocities) vs (broadening/linewidth) contributions may shift quantitatively.

If a different interatomic potential or quench protocol yields a markedly different vibrational density of states (e.g., different low-frequency boson peak character), the threshold x for the transition from localization-dominated to broadening-dominated behavior may change.

supporting_evidence.text: Room-temperature amorphous SiGe: a-Si κ ≈ 2.2 W/mK; 5% Ge reduces κ by ~0.6 W/mK (to ~1.6 W/mK) and 15% Ge reduces it by an additional ~0.55 W/mK (to ~1.05 W/mK), implying a steep initial drop then diminishing returns at higher x.

Mode-resolved contribution: in a-Si the lowest ~8% of modes (0–4 THz in a-Si) contribute ~half of κ; these low-frequency contributions are the ones most strongly suppressed by small Ge concentrations.

Mechanism attribution at low x: κ reduction at low x is reported to be dominated by localization and reduced generalized velocities/spatial overlap rather than a large reduction in lifetimes (i.e., not primarily a crystalline-like mass-scattering-MFP picture).

Mechanism attribution at higher x: at higher Ge concentrations, spectral broadening (linewidth increase) reduces resonant transport and mode diffusivity; high-frequency localization contributes little to total κ due to small heat-carrying weight.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Localization/broadening-controlled thermal transport in glasses and the propagon/diffuson framework are established concepts in amorphous heat transport.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: A compositional-regime law for a-SiGe that (i) identifies a low-x localization/generalized-velocity suppression regime specifically tied to the lowest-frequency mode subset that carries ~O(1) fraction of κ, and (ii) posits a crossover toward broadening/diffusivity control at higher x, with predictive implications for κ(x) curvature and simulation-size sensitivity.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: The underlying mechanisms exist in glass theory, but the statement operationalizes them as a composition-dependent predictive rule for amorphous SiGe specifically, grounded in the provided modal-analysis evidence.
references: Lundgren et al. (2020) [Amorphous Si1-xGex: κ(x) trends, modal localization, generalized velocities; basis for low-x vs higher-x mechanisms]

law.statement_name: Low-frequency convergence law: finite-size dependence in amorphous κ is dominated by the lowest-frequency sector
law.theory_statement: For periodic-supercell MD/QHGK calculations of κ in amorphous Si1-xGex near 300 K, apparent system-size dependence of κ is primarily due to under-sampling/under-resolution of the lowest-frequency modes (in the a-Si reference, roughly <4 THz / lowest ~8% of modes) that contribute disproportionately to κ. Increasing supercell size chiefly increases the resolved contribution from this low-frequency sector; higher-frequency contributions converge at smaller sizes.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: If an amorphous SiGe simulation box is too small, the missing piece is mainly the lowest-frequency heat transport, so κ looks size-dependent for that reason.
law.domain_scope: Amorphous Si1-xGex modeled in periodic bulk supercells using equilibrium MD Green–Kubo (with cepstral analysis) and/or QHGK lattice dynamics near 300 K; applies when vibrational mode discretization and low-frequency density of states are sensitive to finite supercell size.
special_cases: If strong extrinsic scattering is introduced (e.g., explicit free surfaces, pores, or very strong additional disorder) that truncates coherence lengths below the smallest simulated box, size dependence may be weak even in small cells.
In nonequilibrium MD with strong imposed gradients or non-periodic boundaries, additional finite-size artifacts can appear beyond the spectral-resolution effect described here.

supporting_evidence.text: Finite-size effects reported: low-frequency modal contributions (<4 THz in a-Si) show the largest finite-size sensitivity; 1728-atom models differ from converged 13824-atom results mostly in the <4 THz region.

Convergence statement: small cells are adequate for qualitative trends but underconverged for low-frequency quantitative contributions, indicating that κ size dependence is a low-frequency convergence issue.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Finite-size effects in MD thermal conductivity and the special difficulty of converging long-wavelength/low-frequency contributions are well known in general.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The statement specifies, for amorphous SiGe in particular, which spectral sector dominates the size dependence and links it directly to the same low-frequency sector responsible for the strong low-x compositional sensitivity, yielding a practical convergence diagnostic.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: This is a system-specific instantiation of a known MD-convergence issue, made predictive for amorphous SiGe based on the provided modal evidence.
references: Lundgren et al. (2020) [Explicit identification of <4 THz sector as size-sensitive in a-SiGe]

new_predictions_likely: Reverse-NEMD (or EMD) κ for amorphous Si0.5Ge0.5 will show substantially weaker length dependence than crystalline Si0.5Ge0.5 in comparable cell geometries; any residual length dependence should primarily appear as κ increasing with length as the low-frequency sector becomes better represented.

For amorphous Si1-xGex near 300 K, κ(x) will be locally concave upward near x=0 (steep initial drop then diminishing returns), and the composition at which the slope noticeably flattens will correlate with when the lowest-frequency sector’s contribution has already been strongly suppressed.
new_predictions_unknown: Introducing nanometer-scale stiff inclusions (e.g., SiC) into amorphous SiGe could either increase κ (if inclusions create percolating extended vibrational pathways) or decrease κ (if interfaces create additional localization/broadening); the sign should depend on inclusion connectivity and interface bonding strength.

If an ML potential reproduces the amorphous vibrational spectrum more accurately than Tersoff (especially low-frequency modes), it may shift the predicted crossover composition between localization-dominated and broadening-dominated regimes, changing κ(x) curvature while preserving the qualitative early-drop behavior.
negative_experiments: If mode-resolved analysis in amorphous SiGe shows that the lowest-frequency modes remain similarly extended and retain their generalized velocities up to ~10–15% Ge while κ still drops sharply, then localization/reduced generalized-velocity suppression is not the dominant low-x mechanism and the theory fails.

If κ computed in amorphous SiGe decreases systematically with increasing simulation cell size after robust statistical convergence (contrary to the claim that missing low-frequency contributions are added with size), the finite-size law is wrong or incomplete.
If κ(x) in amorphous SiGe is found to be nearly linear in x over 0–20% Ge (no strong early drop), the proposed two-regime compositional mechanism is undermined.

unaccounted_for.text: All crystalline SiGe phenomena in the evidence set (e.g., nanodot barriers, planar superlattices, nanocrystalline grain-boundary transmission, nanoparticle scattering in crystals) are outside this theory’s scope, which is limited to fully amorphous networks.

special_cases: Classical MD at 300 K does not include quantum heat capacities; QHGK introduces quantum heat capacities/populations, so absolute κ values across methods should be compared cautiously even when qualitative κ(x) trends agree.
Very small supercells may spuriously enhance localization simply due to discretization; thus the low-x localization effect should be verified with cells large enough to converge the <4 THz sector.

references: Lundgren et al. (2020) [Amorphous Si1-xGex: κ(x), localization, spectral broadening; provides system-specific basis]
Allen and Feldman (1993) [Diffusons/locons framework; general glass thermal transport theory closely related conceptually]
existing_theory.what_already_exists: Glass thermal transport theories already emphasize localization, diffusons, and spectral broadening as controlling mechanisms rather than crystalline phonon MFPs.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: A composition-regime (low-x vs higher-x) predictive framing for amorphous SiGe that ties (i) the steep initial κ drop to suppression of the lowest-frequency sector carrying ~half of κ in a-Si and (ii) the primary origin of finite-size artifacts to that same sector.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: It is not a new fundamental transport theory for glasses, but it is a novel, testable consolidation into regime-based laws tailored to amorphous SiGe composition trends and MD/QHGK convergence behavior evidenced in the provided study.

theory-6.name: Barrier morphology additivity theory (nanodot layers behave as DMM-like independent resistors)
theory-6.description: In crystalline Si-based multilayers containing Ge nanodot (3D topographic) barrier layers, cross-plane lattice thermal transport is dominated by strongly diffusive phonon scattering at each nanodot barrier. Because long phonon mean free paths in the Si spacers make spacers comparatively low-resistance (often quasi-ballistic over the spacer thickness), the multilayer’s total cross-plane thermal resistance can be approximated as an additive sum of per-barrier resistances plus a smaller spacer/bulk term. Nanodot morphology drives per-barrier scattering closer to the diffuse mismatch model (DMM) limit by introducing nm-scale height/lateral roughness that couples to and suppresses longer-wavelength (low-frequency) heat-carrying phonons more effectively than planar, compositionally disordered SiGe barriers. Consequently, once barriers are in this highly diffusive regime, κ is governed primarily by barrier density (period length / number of barriers) and the per-barrier resistance, and is comparatively less sensitive to the exact Si/Ge volume fraction within the modest Ge-fraction regimes explored experimentally (overall Ge volume fraction <~20%).
theory-6.theory_query: Build theories of how alloy composition, carbon (substitutional or as SiC nanoinclusions), grain boundaries, biaxial strain, amorphisation and the choice of interatomic potential (Tersoff empirical potential, machine-learned potentials, DFT-based Boltzmann transport) affect the lattice thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex and nanostructured SiGeC semiconductors, based on the following results.

components.theory_name_plain_language: Nanodot layers act like separate diffuse scattering barriers that add up
components.theory_description: In crystalline Si-based multilayers containing Ge nanodot (3D topographic) barrier layers, cross-plane lattice thermal transport is dominated by strongly diffusive phonon scattering at each nanodot barrier. Because long phonon mean free paths in the Si spacers make spacers comparatively low-resistance (often quasi-ballistic over the spacer thickness), the multilayer’s total cross-plane thermal resistance can be approximated as an additive sum of per-barrier resistances plus a smaller spacer/bulk term. Nanodot morphology drives per-barrier scattering closer to the diffuse mismatch model (DMM) limit by introducing nm-scale height/lateral roughness that couples to and suppresses longer-wavelength (low-frequency) heat-carrying phonons more effectively than planar, compositionally disordered SiGe barriers. components.theory_description_plain_language: Each nanodot layer behaves like a strong, diffuse phonon-scattering wall. Heat resistance is roughly the sum of the walls, and nanodots reduce thermal conductivity more than flat alloy layers because they scatter long-wavelength phonons better.

law.statement_name: Independent-resistor additivity for highly diffusive nanodot barriers
law.theory_statement: For cross-plane phonon transport through crystalline multilayers in which each barrier layer produces near-diffuse phonon transmission/reflection (DMM-like), the total thermal resistance is approximately additive: R_tot ≈ Σ_i R_barrier,i + R_spacers (often simplified as R_tot ≈ N·R_barrier + R_spacers for nominally identical barriers). Therefore κ_eff decreases monotonically with increasing barrier density (decreasing period length or increasing N at fixed total thickness) until (i) spacer resistance dominates, or (ii) barriers saturate at a maximum diffusive resistance set by modal mismatch and local disorder/topography.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: If each nanodot layer scatters diffusively, adding more layers adds resistance almost linearly, so thermal conductivity drops as the barrier layers get denser—until spacer resistance or saturation limits further drops.
law.domain_scope: Cross-plane lattice thermal transport in crystalline Si matrices with embedded Ge nanodot (3D island/topographic) barrier layers at ~room temperature, in the incoherent (non-wave-interference-dominated) regime where barriers act as independent scatterers and Si spacer thickness is not so small that coherent minibands dominate. Applies to nanodot multilayers similar to those measured by HPTR/differential 3ω and simulated by AGF with dot self-energy approximations.
special_cases: If barrier layers are not strongly diffusive (partially specular interfaces, low roughness, or weak disorder), barrier resistances are not independent and additivity can fail.

If period lengths become so short that coherent interference/miniband formation becomes important (ultrashort periods; not evidenced in the cited nanodot samples down to ~3.7 nm period), additivity can break down and κ may show non-monotonic period dependence.

If barriers introduce significant correlated long-range strain fields that couple barriers over multiple periods, an additional non-additive component may appear (not quantified in the supporting evidence).

supporting_evidence.text: Experiments on epitaxial Si with vertically stacked Ge nanodot layers report that transport is ballistic in Si spacers (due to long phonon MFPs) while scattering is dominated by independent nanodot layers, so total resistance is interpreted as the sum of barrier resistances; measured κ_cross-plane reaches (0.9 ± 0.1) W/m-K for a ~15.5 nm region with 5 nanodot layers and ~3.7 nm period, and per-barrier resistances are discussed as additive and DMM-like.

AGF simulations of nanodot-barrier multilayers yield conductivities close to the DMM limit and in reasonable agreement with experiment, supporting the assumption that each nanodot barrier behaves as a highly diffusive scatterer whose resistance can be treated in an incoherent/additive manner at the device scale (within modeling approximations).

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Resistance additivity in incoherent multilayers and the concept of DMM-like limiting behavior at highly diffusive interfaces are established in nanoscale thermal transport and are widely used for multilayer/superlattice interpretation.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The statement elevates nanodot (3D topographic) morphology as a practical criterion for when barrier layers enter a regime where DMM-like independent-resistor additivity becomes predictive, distinguishing it from planar alloy barriers that remain less diffusive for key low-frequency modes.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: The components (additivity; DMM limit) are known, but the morphology-triggered regime-switch framing is a more explicit, design-oriented rule abstracted from the nanodot vs flat-barrier comparisons in the provided evidence.
references: Ravichandran et al. (2014) Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers [interprets nanodot layers as highly diffusive barriers with additive resistances; close-to-DMM behavior]
Swartz and Pohl (1989) Thermal boundary resistance [foundational interface-resistance concepts underlying additivity/DMM-limit thinking]
Cahill et al. (2003) Nanoscale thermal transport [review context for DMM-like limits and interface-dominated multilayers]

law.statement_name: Nanodot morphology enhances low-frequency scattering relative to flat disordered alloy barriers
law.theory_statement: At comparable average mass contrast/alloying, nanodot (3D, nm-topography) barriers reduce κ_cross-plane more than planar SiGe alloy barriers because nanodot morphology introduces larger lateral and height length scales that couple to long-wavelength (low-frequency) phonons. These low-frequency modes can otherwise transmit efficiently across planar compositionally disordered barriers, but become strongly scattered when the interface becomes topographically rough and spatially nonuniform at length scales comparable to their wavelengths or to transverse coherence lengths. The practical signature is that nanodot-barrier κ approaches DMM-like values, whereas flat-barrier κ remains higher under similar composition contrast.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: Nanodots scatter long-wavelength phonons better than flat alloy layers, so they reduce thermal conductivity more and push behavior toward a diffuse-interface limit.
law.domain_scope: Crystalline Si/Ge nanostructures where the comparison is between (i) planar, compositionally disordered SiGe barriers and (ii) nanodot/lens-shaped Ge barrier layers embedded in Si; primarily cross-plane transport at ~room temperature under conditions where transport is interface/barrier dominated. Also applies qualitatively to other systems where introducing 3D roughness at barriers increases low-frequency phonon scattering.
special_cases: If planar barriers already possess comparable roughness/intermixing length scales (e.g., severe interdiffusion/roughness), the incremental advantage of nanodots may diminish.

If nanoparticle/nanodot strain fields (elastic mismatch) become large and long-ranged, strain-induced changes to dispersion and additional scattering could contribute beyond pure morphology; in the cited first-principles nanoparticle work, strain effects were estimated small for Si/Ge nanoparticles and neglected (so this law focuses on morphology/mass-disorder-driven scattering).

supporting_evidence.text: AGF calculations explicitly comparing flat Si0.5Ge0.5 barriers to lens-shaped nanodot barriers show the nanodot systems yield significantly lower κ and are close to DMM and experiments, while flat barriers yield higher κ. The mechanism attributed is that nanodots introduce larger-scale roughness features that reduce low-frequency phonon mean free paths relative to flat disordered interfaces; high-frequency behavior is more similar between flat and nanodot cases.

Experiments on epitaxial Ge nanodot multilayers in Si report very low κ_cross-plane (down to ~0.9 W/m-K) and interpret the nanodot layers as highly diffusive barriers consistent with DMM-like limits; the paper contrasts this with prior flat-barrier superlattice literature that exhibits higher κ/less diffusive behavior.

Compositionally modulated SiGe multilayers (graded/interdiffused planar profiles) are predicted and measured to achieve κ lower than abrupt-barrier or homogeneous-alloy limits because combining barrier-like scattering (effective at low frequencies) with alloy disorder (effective at high frequencies) broadens the scattered frequency range. This supports the broader principle that adding structural nonuniformity that targets low-frequency phonons can outperform purely planar composition disorder alone.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: That interface roughness/topography increases phonon scattering and that low-frequency phonons are harder to scatter with purely atomic-scale disorder are established ideas in nanoscale thermal transport.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The statement consolidates a specific, experimentally supported hierarchy—nanodot topography drives systems toward DMM-like limits and reduces κ relative to flat alloy barriers by preferentially impacting low-frequency modes—into a design rule that distinguishes morphology classes rather than only interface ‘roughness’ in the abstract.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Mechanism is consistent with existing roughness-scattering concepts, but the evidence-backed linkage between nanodot morphology, low-frequency MFP suppression, and DMM-proximate κ provides a more actionable, morphology-specific predictive rule.
references: Ravichandran et al. (2014) Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers [nanodot layers yield near-DMM behavior and much lower κ than flatter interfaces]
Kim et al. (interface roughness literature, various years) [general roughness-enhanced phonon scattering concepts]
Luckyanova et al. (2012) Coherent phonon heat conduction in superlattices [contrasting coherent regime vs diffuse/rough regime boundary]

new_predictions_likely: Keeping total Ge volume fraction fixed (<~20%) in an epitaxial Si matrix, converting planar SiGe barrier layers into nanodot (3D topographic) barrier layers will reduce κ_cross-plane and move the measured per-barrier resistance closer to full-dispersion DMM estimates; the effect will be strongest at room temperature where long-MFP acoustic modes contribute substantially.

At fixed dot morphology and similar dot size distribution, κ_cross-plane will approximately follow R_tot ≈ N·R_barrier + R_spacers: doubling the number of nanodot layers (at similar spacers) will increase total resistance approximately linearly until spacer resistance becomes non-negligible.

If dot morphology is progressively smoothed (e.g., annealing that rounds features and reduces height variation without changing average Ge content much), κ_cross-plane will increase toward the planar-barrier trend, with the largest relative recovery in contributions from low-frequency modes.
new_predictions_unknown: If nanodot barrier layers are partially amorphized (confined to dot regions) while spacers remain crystalline, per-barrier resistance may increase beyond the DMM-like crystalline-interface limit by adding localized vibrational states; whether κ decreases further or saturates depends on whether the current nanodot layers are already near the maximum diffusive scattering attainable for the dominant low-frequency modes.

Applying coherent biaxial strain to the Si spacer regions (without introducing dislocations) could either increase or decrease R_barrier depending on how strain shifts acoustic mismatch and mode conversion at the dot/spacer interface; a sign change with temperature is possible if different spectral regions dominate at different T.
negative_experiments: Measure κ_cross-plane for otherwise identical multilayers while varying only the number of nanodot layers N at fixed total thickness (compensating spacer thickness accordingly). If R_tot is not approximately linear in N in the regime where barriers are claimed to be independent, the additivity assumption is falsified.

Create a planar-barrier multilayer engineered to have similar roughness amplitude/correlation lengths as the nanodot case (e.g., intentionally roughened planar interfaces). If κ matches the nanodot case, then nanodot-specific morphology is not the controlling factor; if κ remains higher, it supports the unique low-frequency scattering role of true 3D topography.

Perform spectral/size-sensitive measurements (e.g., varying spacer thickness systematically) to see whether the inferred per-barrier resistance is constant. Strong spacer-thickness dependence of extracted R_barrier would indicate non-independent barriers or coherent effects.

unaccounted_for.text: The theory does not address substitutional carbon in SiGe, SiC nanoinclusions, or carbon-driven local chemical ordering (Si-rich shells), which are central to other hypotheses in the mission statement but absent from the nanodot evidence base here.

The theory does not attempt to explain amorphous SiGe thermal conductivity trends or localization physics in glasses, which involve different mechanisms than interface/barrier-dominated crystalline multilayers.

special_cases: Ultrashort periods where coherent interference/minibands can arise: additivity may fail and κ may become non-monotonic with period (not observed down to ~3.7 nm in the cited nanodot multilayers).
Very thick spacers (spacer thickness comparable to or exceeding dominant phonon MFPs): spacer resistance becomes important and κ is no longer set primarily by N·R_barrier.
If barriers are not diffusive (high specularity), barrier resistances are not independent and DMM-like behavior is not expected.

references: Ravichandran et al. (2014) Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers [empirical basis for DMM-like, additive nanodot barriers]
Swartz and Pohl (1989) Thermal boundary resistance [establishes interface resistance concepts underlying additivity]
Chen (2005) Nanoscale Energy Transport and Conversion [textbook foundation for DMM limits and series thermal resistances]
existing_theory.what_already_exists: Diffuse interface scattering, DMM limits, and series-additive thermal resistances are well-established for incoherent multilayers and interface-dominated transport.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: A morphology-specific predictive framing: nanodot/topographic barriers act as a switch that broadens scattering into low-frequency modes, pushing multilayers into a DMM-like additive-barrier regime more effectively than planar alloy barriers.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: This is not a new fundamental transport law, but a sharpened, design-relevant criterion abstracted from the provided nanodot experiment + AGF comparison evidence.

components.mission_statement:
The theories will be used to answer the following questions before the corresponding simulation results are seen. Address the mechanisms they depend on:

H1. Two 3C-SiC spheres of radius R are embedded in Si0.8Ge0.2 (Tersoff MD,
300 K, reverse NEMD). A continuum scattering model brackets the particle's
effect on lattice thermal conductivity between a density-contrast-only lower
bound and a stiffness-contrast-only upper bound. At R = 2.0 nm the bracket is
a 40 % to 75 % reduction of kappa relative to the same alloy without the
particle (with the surrounding composition held equal).
Category for the MD result at R = 2.0 nm: "below", "inside", "above".
Value: the MD reduction in percent.
H1b. In the same set-up, carbon prefers Si neighbours, so the control runs
place each particle inside a Si-rich (Ge-free) shell about 7 A thick. Does a
run with particle plus Si-rich shell conduct heat better or worse than the
bare Si0.8Ge0.2 alloy with neither?
Category: "higher", "lower". Value: percent change of kappa relative to the
bare alloy, for R = 2.0 nm.
H2. A symbolic law for Tersoff-MD kappa of Si1-xGex, of the form
kappa = 1/(a + b x + c x^2 + d T), was fitted on 0.05 <= x <= 0.93 at
finite box size. Points at x > 0.93 sit well above the law and an outlier
detector flagged two of them as isolated faults. At x = 0.90, 300 K, the
same box gives kappa = 4.5 W/mK.
Category: "fault" (the high points are errors), "physics" (they are real).
Value: kappa at x = 0.97, 300 K in the same box, W/mK.
H3. almaBTE (virtual crystal, DFT force constants, full iterative BTE)
gives kappa of bulk Si1-xGex in W/mK:

| x | 300 K | 700 K | 1100 K |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 160.5 | 63.8 | 40.5 |
| 0.15 | 8.33 | 6.69 | 5.72 |
| 0.2 | 7.27 | 5.89 | 5.07 |
| 0.5 | 6.49 | 5.08 | 4.30 |
| 0.85 | 11.54 | 7.83 | 6.21 |
| 1 | 57.1 | 25.7 | 16.7 |

Value: almaBTE kappa at x = 0.7, 1100 K (W/mK). Category: where is the
composition of minimum kappa at 1100 K: "x<0.4", "0.4<=x<=0.6", "x>0.6".
H4. Amorphous Si0.5Ge0.5 is made by melt-quenching with the Tersoff
potential and kappa is computed by reverse NEMD in boxes of three lengths
(24, 48 and 96 conventional cells along the heat-flow direction, 4 x 4
cells across). Crystalline alloy kappa in these boxes rises with length.
Category: "size-independent", "rises with length", "falls with length".
Value: ratio kappa(96 cells)/kappa(24 cells).
H5. Pure crystalline Si: Tersoff-1989 GPUMD homogeneous NEMD kappa versus
almaBTE (160.5 W/mK at 300 K, 40.5 W/mK at 1100 K).
Value: ratio Tersoff/almaBTE at 300 K. Category for 1100 K:
"agree within 30 %", "Tersoff higher by more than 30 %",
"Tersoff lower by more than 30 %".
H6. Ball-milled and sintered Si0.8Ge0.2 with 1 at% carbon. MACE-MP-0
energies compare a substitutional C atom in the alloy with the same C atom
moved into a SiC precipitate.
Category: "SiC precipitate favoured", "substitutional favoured".
Value: energy gained per C atom by forming SiC, eV (positive = SiC
favoured). Also give, inside "theory", whether C prefers Si or Ge
neighbours and by how much (eV).
H7. A Si0.5Ge0.5 film is grown coherently on Si(001) (biaxial in-plane
compression of about 2 %) and kappa is computed by Tersoff MD in-plane and
across the film, compared with relaxed bulk Si0.5Ge0.5.
Category for the cross-plane change at 300 K: "increase", "decrease",
"no change within 5 %". Value: cross-plane change at 300 K in percent.
State in "theory" what happens in-plane.
H8. Starrydata2 holds digitized kappa of sintered (hot-pressed or spark
plasma sintered) Si0.8Ge0.2, many papers. almaBTE perfect-crystal kappa at
x = 0.2, 300 K is 7.27 W/mK.
Value: median ratio of sintered lattice kappa to the almaBTE value at
300 K. Category: "below 0.7", "0.7 to 0.9", "above 0.9".
O3. If the carbon-location calculation of H6 is repeated with a newer
foundation potential trained on more data (for example a MACE model trained
on MPtrj plus Alexandria), does the sign of the SiC-precipitation energy
hold? Category: "sign holds, magnitude within 0.3 eV", "sign holds,
magnitude changes by more than 0.3 eV", "sign flips". Value: predicted
energy gained per C atom, eV.

metadata.title: Diameter dependence of SiGe nanowire thermal conductivity
metadata.abstract: We theoretically compute the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloy nanowires as a function of nanowire diameter, alloy concentration, and temperature, obtaining a satisfactory quantitative agreement with experimental results. Our results account for the weaker diameter dependence of the thermal conductivity recently observed in Si$_{1-x}$Ge$_x$ nanowires ($x<0.1$), as compared to pure Si nanowires. We also present calculations in the full range of alloy concentrations, $0 \leq x \leq 1$, which may serve as a basis for comparison with future experiments on high alloy concentration nanowires.

metadata.title: The best nanoparticle size distribution for minimum thermal conductivity

tldr.text: This work uses optimization methods to show that the best nanoparticle size distribution to scatter the broad thermal phonon spectrum is not a similarly broad distribution but rather several discrete peaks at well-chosen nanoparticle radii.

metadata.abstract: Which sizes of nanoparticles embedded in a crystalline solid yield the lowest thermal conductivity? Nanoparticles have long been demonstrated to reduce the thermal conductivity of crystals by scattering phonons, but most previous works assumed the nanoparticles to have a single size. Here, we use optimization methods to show that the best nanoparticle size distribution to scatter the broad thermal phonon spectrum is not a similarly broad distribution but rather several discrete peaks at well-chosen nanoparticle radii. For SiGe, the best size distribution yields a thermal conductivity below that of amorphous silicon. Further, we demonstrate that a simplified distribution yields nearly the same low thermal conductivity and can be readily fabricated. Our work provides important insights into how to manipulate the full spectrum of phonons and will guide the design of more efficient thermoelectric materials.

| alloy_and_defect_scattering_model | Alloy point defects (individual Ge atoms) are treated using the approach of Garg et al. (mass-defect scattering dominant) — Ge atoms treated as independent point-defects. Nanoparticle scattering rate uses an analytic interpolating model: τ_np^{-1} = v (σ_s^{-1} + σ_l^{-1})^{-1} n, with σ_s = 2πR^2 (short-wavelength/geometric limit) and σ_l = (4/3)π R^3 (Δρ/ρ)^2 (ω R / v)^4 (long-wavelength Rayleigh-like limit), where Δρ is density difference and n is number density of nanoparticles. Matthiessen's rule is used to combine scattering. The model neglects changes in interatomic force constants between Si and SiGe and assumes mass difference is dominant. |
| strain_effects_on_phonons | No biaxial or other strain effects analyzed; strain is not treated in this work. |
| microstructure_mechanisms_claimed | Primary mechanisms: mass-difference (mass disorder) scattering from point defects and nanoparticles that reduce phonon lifetimes and mean free paths; geometric scattering from larger nanoparticles (short-wavelength/particle-size scattering) and Rayleigh-like frequency-dependent scattering for long wavelengths; grain boundaries scattering long-MFP phonons (phenomenological τ_grain). Authors assert force-constant changes are negligible compared to mass-difference (citing prior first-principles work). They explain that discrete nanoparticle radii selectively scatter different phonon frequency bands, so a few non-adjacent radii optimize scattering across the broad phonon spectrum. |
| key_comparisons_and_counterexamples | Comparisons made between Debye, BvK, and full DFT dispersions (all give similar optimal discrete-peak size distributions); comparison to single-size nanoparticle-in-alloy strategy of Mingo et al. (Ref. 9) — best-distribution yields k much lower (factor >3) than Mingo-style; comparison to amorphous Si (a-Si k ≈ 1.5 W/mK) used as benchmark — optimized distributions can achieve k below a-Si for sufficient Ge concentration; grain-boundary inclusion reduces k further for some concentration ranges (e.g., L = 20 nm, x = 12.2% gives k = 2.5 W/mK vs 2.6 W/mK at 17% without grain boundaries). No carbon/substitutional-C or SiC-inclusion cases are considered in this paper. |
| reported_uncertainties_and_limitations | Authors note approximations and limitations: (1) nanoparticle scattering model is simplified and neglects changes in interatomic force constants between Si and SiGe (justified by prior work claiming mass-difference dominance), (2) the analytic scattering model matches exact scattering calculations to within ~20% (cited), (3) largest nanoparticle size was capped at R = 5.44 nm to avoid complicated intra-particle transport physics, (4) grain-boundary treatment is phenomenological (τ_grain = v/L) and does not include explicit GB atomistics or TBR values, (5) details of ShengBTE calculation settings (q-mesh, supercell sizes, 2nd/3rd order FCs) are not provided in the paper text. |
| figures_or_tables_with_primary_results | Fig. 1 (optimal nanoparticle size distribution for 1% Ge for Debye/BvK/DFT), Fig. 2 (optimized size distributions for Ge% = 0.1%, 12.2%, 50.8%), Fig. 3 (a: \|dk/dx\| vs x for several radii; b: nanoparticle scattering rate vs phonon frequency), Fig. 4 (optimal size distributions with grain sizes L = 100 nm and 20 nm for Ge concentrations 12.2% and 50.8%), Fig. 5 (a: k vs total Ge concentration for best distribution, Mingo ref strategy, and modified single-size strategy; b: nanoparticle radius and fraction of Ge in nanoparticles vs total Ge concentration). |

metadata.title: Mode localization and suppressed heat transport in amorphous alloys
metadata.abstract: Glasses usually represent the lower limit for the thermal conductivity of solids, but a fundamental understanding of lattice heat transport in amorphous materials can provide design rules to beat such a limit. Here we investigate the role of mass disorder in glasses by studying amorphous silicon-germanium alloy (a-${\mathrm{Si}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Ge}}_{x}$) over the full range of atomic concentration from $x=0$ to $x=1$, using molecular dynamics and the quasiharmonic Green-Kubo lattice dynamics formalism. We find that the thermal conductivity of a-${\mathrm{Si}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Ge}}_{x}$ as a function of $x$ exhibits a smoother U shape than in crystalline mass-disordered alloys. The main contribution to the initial drop of thermal conductivity at low Ge concentration stems from the localization of otherwise extended modes that make up the lowest 8% of the population by frequency. Contributions from intermediate frequency modes are decreased more gradually with increasing Ge to reach a broad minimum thermal conductivity between concentrations of Ge from $x=0.25$ to 0.75. Modal analysis unravels the correlations among localization, line broadening, and the contribution to thermal transport of modes within different frequency ranges.

metadata.title: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.

tldr.text: By engineering a set of individual phonon-scattering nanodot barriers, this work accurately tailored the thermal conductivity of a single-crystalline SiGe material in spatially defined regions as short as approximately 15 nm, resulting in a room-temperature kappa well below the amorphous limit.

metadata.abstract: The ability to precisely control the thermal conductivity (kappa) of a material is fundamental in the development of on-chip heat management or energy conversion applications. Nanostructuring permits a marked reduction of kappa of single-crystalline materials, as recently demonstrated for silicon nanowires. However, silicon-based nanostructured materials with extremely low kappa are not limited to nanowires. By engineering a set of individual phonon-scattering nanodot barriers we have accurately tailored the thermal conductivity of a single-crystalline SiGe material in spatially defined regions as short as approximately 15 nm. Single-barrier thermal resistances between 2 and 4 x 10(-9) m(2) K W(-1) were attained, resulting in a room-temperature kappa down to about 0.9 W m(-1) K(-1), in multilayered structures with as little as five barriers. Such low thermal conductivity is compatible with a totally diffuse mismatch model for the barriers, and it is well below the amorphous limit. The results are in agreement with atomistic Green's function simulations.

metadata.title: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art
metadata.abstract: In our environment, the large availability of wasted heat has motivated the search for methods to harvest heat. As a reliable way to supply energy, SiGe has been used for thermoelectric generators (TEGs) in space missions for decades. Recently, micro-thermoelectric generators (μTEG) have been shown to be a promising way to supply energy for the Internet of Things (IoT) by using daily waste heat. Combining the predominant CMOS compatibility with high electric conductivity and low thermal conductivity performance, Si nanowire and SiGe nanowire have been a candidate for μTEG. This review gives a comprehensive introduction of the Si, SiGe nanowires, and their possibility for μTEG. The basic thermoelectric principles, materials, structures, fabrication, measurements, and applications are discussed in depth.
