paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db2.displayLabel: Compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivity below the thin-film alloy limit

s2Metadata.title: Compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivity below the thin-film alloy limit
s2Metadata.abstract: We describe epitaxial Ge/Si multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivities which can be systematically reduced to exceptionally low values, as compared both with bulk and thin-film SiGe alloys of the same average concentration, by simply changing the thicknesses of the constituent layers. Ab initio calculations reveal that partial interdiffusion of Ge into the Si spacers, which naturally results from Ge segregation during growth, plays a determinant role, lowering the thermal conductivity below what could be achieved without interdiffusion (perfect superlattice), or with total interdiffusion (alloy limit). This phenomenon is similar to the one previously observed in alloys with embedded nanoparticles, and it stresses the importance of combining alloy and nanosized scatterers simultaneously to minimize thermal conductivity. Our calculations thus suggest that superlattices with sharp interfaces, which are commonly sought but difficult to realize, are worse than compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers in the search for materials with ultralow thermal conductivities.

paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880ce.displayLabel: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.

s2Metadata.title: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.
s2Metadata.abstract: The ability to precisely control the thermal conductivity (kappa) of a material is fundamental in the development of on-chip heat management or energy conversion applications. Nanostructuring permits a marked reduction of kappa of single-crystalline materials, as recently demonstrated for silicon nanowires. However, silicon-based nanostructured materials with extremely low kappa are not limited to nanowires. By engineering a set of individual phonon-scattering nanodot barriers we have accurately tailored the thermal conductivity of a single-crystalline SiGe material in spatially defined regions as short as approximately 15 nm. Single-barrier thermal resistances between 2 and 4 x 10(-9) m(2) K W(-1) were attained, resulting in a room-temperature kappa down to about 0.9 W m(-1) K(-1), in multilayered structures with as little as five barriers. Such low thermal conductivity is compatible with a totally diffuse mismatch model for the barriers, and it is well below the amorphous limit. The results are in agreement with atomistic Green's function simulations.

paper-819408632f51db9848aa8f2b19705eeff4.displayLabel: Diameter dependence of SiGe nanowire thermal conductivity

s2Metadata.title: Diameter dependence of SiGe nanowire thermal conductivity
s2Metadata.abstract: We theoretically compute the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloy nanowires as a function of nanowire diameter, alloy concentration, and temperature, obtaining a satisfactory quantitative agreement with experimental results. Our results account for the weaker diameter dependence of the thermal conductivity recently observed in Si$_{1-x}$Ge$_x$ nanowires ($x<0.1$), as compared to pure Si nanowires. We also present calculations in the full range of alloy concentrations, $0 \leq x \leq 1$, which may serve as a basis for comparison with future experiments on high alloy concentration nanowires.

paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6.displayLabel: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art

s2Metadata.title: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art
s2Metadata.abstract: In our environment, the large availability of wasted heat has motivated the search for methods to harvest heat. As a reliable way to supply energy, SiGe has been used for thermoelectric generators (TEGs) in space missions for decades. Recently, micro-thermoelectric generators (μTEG) have been shown to be a promising way to supply energy for the Internet of Things (IoT) by using daily waste heat. Combining the predominant CMOS compatibility with high electric conductivity and low thermal conductivity performance, Si nanowire and SiGe nanowire have been a candidate for μTEG. This review gives a comprehensive introduction of the Si, SiGe nanowires, and their possibility for μTEG. The basic thermoelectric principles, materials, structures, fabrication, measurements, and applications are discussed in depth.

paper-3b9d56c73fcc42f28b31eab8ade7dd5068.displayLabel: Thermal transport in nanocrystalline Si and SiGe by ab initio based Monte Carlo simulation

s2Metadata.title: Thermal transport in nanocrystalline Si and SiGe by ab initio based Monte Carlo simulation
s2Metadata.abstract: Nanocrystalline thermoelectric materials based on Si have long been of interest because Si is earth-abundant, inexpensive, and non-toxic. However, a poor understanding of phonon grain boundary scattering and its effect on thermal conductivity has impeded efforts to improve the thermoelectric figure of merit. Here, we report an ab-initio based computational study of thermal transport in nanocrystalline Si-based materials using a variance-reduced Monte Carlo method with the full phonon dispersion and intrinsic lifetimes from first-principles as input. By fitting the transmission profile of grain boundaries, we obtain excellent agreement with experimental thermal conductivity of nanocrystalline Si [Wang et al. Nano Letters 11, 2206 (2011)]. Based on these calculations, we examine phonon transport in nanocrystalline SiGe alloys with ab-initio electron-phonon scattering rates. Our calculations show that low energy phonons still transport substantial amounts of heat in these materials, despite scattering by electron-phonon interactions, due to the high transmission of phonons at grain boundaries, and thus improvements in ZT are still possible by disrupting these modes. This work demonstrates the important insights into phonon transport that can be obtained using ab-initio based Monte Carlo simulations in complex nanostructured materials.

paper-f717d335b5fc0e468f31492d359a2c3a30.displayLabel: The best nanoparticle size distribution for minimum thermal conductivity

s2Metadata.title: The best nanoparticle size distribution for minimum thermal conductivity
s2Metadata.abstract: Which sizes of nanoparticles embedded in a crystalline solid yield the lowest thermal conductivity? Nanoparticles have long been demonstrated to reduce the thermal conductivity of crystals by scattering phonons, but most previous works assumed the nanoparticles to have a single size. Here, we use optimization methods to show that the best nanoparticle size distribution to scatter the broad thermal phonon spectrum is not a similarly broad distribution but rather several discrete peaks at well-chosen nanoparticle radii. For SiGe, the best size distribution yields a thermal conductivity below that of amorphous silicon. Further, we demonstrate that a simplified distribution yields nearly the same low thermal conductivity and can be readily fabricated. Our work provides important insights into how to manipulate the full spectrum of phonons and will guide the design of more efficient thermoelectric materials.

paper-4e8dff46ba90e16bec4eddadf2414abfa3.displayLabel: Unifying first-principles theoretical predictions and experimental measurements of size effects in thermal transport in SiGe alloys

s2Metadata.title: Unifying first-principles theoretical predictions and experimental measurements of size effects in thermal transport in SiGe alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate the correspondence between first principle calculations and experimental measurements of size effects on thermal transport in SiGe alloys. Transient thermal grating (TTG) is used to measure the effective thermal conductivity. The virtual crystal approximation under the density functional theory (DFT) framework combined with impurity scattering is used to determine the phonon properties for the exact alloy composition of the measured samples. With these properties, classical size effects are calculated for the experimental geometry of reflection mode TTG using the recently-developed variational solution to the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE), which is verified against established Monte Carlo simulations. We find agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements in the reduction of thermal conductivity (as much as $\sim$ 25\% of the bulk value) across grating periods spanning one order of magnitude. This work provides a framework for the tabletop study of size effects on thermal transport.

paper-965a7f2bf9c14cba930b172313c764df40.displayLabel: Role of light and heavy embedded nanoparticles on the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloys

s2Metadata.title: Role of light and heavy embedded nanoparticles on the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: We have used an atomistic {\it ab initio} approach with no adjustable parameters to compute the lattice thermal conductivity of Si$_{0.5}$Ge$_{0.5}$ with a low concentration of embedded Si or Ge nanoparticles of diameters up to 4.4 nm. Through exact Green's function calculation of the nanoparticle scattering rates, we find that embedding Ge nanoparticles in $\text{Si}_{0.5}\text{Ge}_{0.5}$ provides 20% lower thermal conductivities than embedding Si nanoparticles. This contrasts with the Born approximation which predicts an equal amount of reduction for the two cases, irrespective of the sign of the mass difference. Despite these differences, we find that the Born approximation still performs remarkably well, and it permits investigation of larger nanoparticle sizes, up to 60 nm in diameter, not feasible with the exact approach.

content.title: Complementary spectral selectivity enables sub-limit kappa in crystalline Si/Ge systems

content.text: Alloy disorder and larger features block different phonons; using both can reduce thermal conductivity more than either alone at the same overall composition.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Compositionally modulated Si1-xGex multilayers exhibit cross-plane kappa values below bulk-alloy values and below a thin-film alloy limit; the accompanying first-principles BTE model explicitly decomposes the scattering potential into a mean mass-density profile M(z) (barrier-like, effective for low-frequency/long-MFP modes) plus local random fluctuations ΔM (alloy-like, effective for high-frequency modes), and attributes the enhanced suppression to simultaneous spectral coverage.  <paper entityId="paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db24d00dd" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="119227704" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Chen et al., 2013</paper>

- Ge nanodot multilayers in Si reach very low room-temperature cross-plane kappa (~0.9 W/mK) and behave close to a DMM-like diffusive limit; the work interprets transport as ballistic within Si spacers with additive, highly diffusive barrier resistances, consistent with strong suppression of long-MFP/low-frequency carriers by nanodot layers.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- AGF simulations comparing nanodot-barrier multilayers vs flat Si0.5Ge0.5 alloy barriers find nanodot systems give significantly lower kappa and are closer to DMM than flat barriers; the interpretation is that dot-induced large-scale roughness increases scattering over a wider (especially low-frequency) range than flat disordered barriers.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- Theory for Si1-xGex nanowires states alloy scattering strongly suppresses high-frequency phonons and leaves low-frequency phonons relatively unaffected, shifting heat to low-frequency long-MFP modes; this explains weaker diameter dependence and stronger length dependence in alloys compared to pure Si, highlighting the need for additional low-frequency suppression mechanisms to further reduce kappa.  <paper entityId="paper-819408632f51db9848aa8f2b19705eeff47ff7e1" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="118592133" artifactId="extraction-result-1#uuid-e1.0">Wang et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.4">Li et al., 2021</paper>

- Nanocrystalline Si and nanocrystalline SiGe (2% Ge) ab-initio-based Monte Carlo modeling shows grain boundaries transmit low-frequency phonons with near-unity transmission below ~2–3 THz while higher-frequency modes are more strongly blocked; this implies GBs alone may not fully suppress the low-frequency band and motivates combining GBs with alloy/defect scattering for broader spectral coverage.  <paper entityId="paper-3b9d56c73fcc42f28b31eab8ade7dd5068c86121" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="14166953" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.1">Yang et al., 2017</paper>

- A first-principles-informed design study for Si with Ge allocated between point defects and nanoparticles (plus optional grain-boundary scattering) shows much lower kappa when multiple scattering channels are combined and tuned to target different spectral regions; the reported strong drop at fixed total Ge fraction when adding nanoparticles (and further with grain boundaries) is consistent with the principle that broader spectral/MFP coverage yields lower kappa than homogeneous alloying alone.  <paper entityId="paper-f717d335b5fc0e468f31492d359a2c3a30f614ee" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="6177564" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Zhang et al., 2014</paper>

- In a single-crystal Si0.934Ge0.066 film, DFT-BTE + TTG interpretation emphasizes that alloy disorder shifts heat to longer-MFP modes, making size/geometry suppression of those modes important; this supports the idea that different mechanisms act on different parts of the spectrum and must be treated spectrally (not by a single gray cutoff).  <paper entityId="paper-4e8dff46ba90e16bec4eddadf2414abfa3ca51e7" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="96453663" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Huberman et al., 2017</paper>

content.title: Non-Born (T-matrix) heavy/light inclusion asymmetry for low-frequency-dominated transport

content.text: Once the remaining heat is mostly carried by low-frequency phonons, heavier nanoparticles can block those phonons more strongly than equally sized lighter nanoparticles, lowering thermal conductivity more.
**Supporting evidence:**

- First-principles iterative BTE + exact atomistic T-matrix scattering for nanoparticles in Si0.5Ge0.5 reports that Ge (heavy) nanoparticles can yield up to ~20% lower kappa than Si (light) nanoparticles at the same size and concentration, and explicitly notes this asymmetry is not captured by the Born approximation (which is symmetric).  <paper entityId="paper-965a7f2bf9c14cba930b172313c764df40c505b5" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="53628875" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Kundu et al., 2011</paper>

- In crystalline Si-rich SiGe (e.g., x~0.2), adding a small volume fraction of nm-scale inclusions will reduce kappa more if the inclusions are heavier-than-host (Ge-rich) than if they are lighter-than-host (Si-rich), provided the inclusion radius is large enough to exit the Born regime (order ~1–5 nm).
- In compositionally modulated multilayers, deliberately combining a graded mean Ge profile M(z) with residual atomic-scale randomness (not perfectly ordered layers) will yield lower cross-plane kappa than either (i) a perfectly abrupt superlattice with minimal interdiffusion (mostly barrier scattering) or (ii) a homogeneous alloy film (mostly ΔM scattering) at the same average Ge fraction.
- For SiGe nanowires, increasing Ge content from very small x will weaken diameter dependence but strengthen length dependence of kappa as the dominant heat-carrying spectrum shifts to low-frequency long-MFP modes, making suppression depend more on axial length/feature spacing than on diameter alone.

- A three-way combination in bulk-like crystalline SiGe—(i) intermediate x to maximize alloy suppression of high-frequency modes, (ii) heavy nanoparticles sized to maximize low-frequency scattering, and (iii) grain boundaries engineered for low-frequency transmission loss—could push room-temperature kappa toward ~1 W/mK without amorphization; success depends on whether low-frequency transmission can be sufficiently reduced without creating percolating high-kappa paths.
- In coherently strained, compositionally modulated SiGe multilayers, biaxial strain could shift which frequencies dominate heat conduction (via group-velocity and anharmonicity changes) and therefore alter the optimal modulation length scale needed for spectral coverage; the direction/magnitude is uncertain without explicit strain-renormalized phonons.

- Construct two samples with identical average Ge fraction and identical mesoscale feature density, but one with (near) perfect ordering (minimal ΔM) and one with strong local randomness (large ΔM). If the more random sample does not show lower kappa (after controlling for porosity/defects), the claimed complementarity of ΔM with mesoscale scattering is weakened.
- Compare heavy vs light nanoparticle inclusions of identical radius and volume fraction in a regime where nm-scale inclusions should be non-Born. If the kappa reductions are equal within uncertainty, the heavy/light asymmetry claim fails (or indicates force-constant/strain effects dominate).
- If a nanodot-barrier system with strong roughness shows no approach toward DMM-like behavior (i.e., remains closer to flat-barrier conductivities), then the claim that mesoscale morphology primarily suppresses low-frequency/long-MFP carriers is called into question.

- Absolute kappa values and quantitative offsets across methods (AGF with mass-difference approximation, empirical-potential MD, and DFT-BTE) are not explained; the theory focuses on qualitative trends and design conditions rather than method-dependent calibration errors.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Pernot et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-4e8dff46ba90e16bec4eddadf2414abfa3ca51e7" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="96453663" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Huberman et al., 2017</paper> <paper entityId="paper-965a7f2bf9c14cba930b172313c764df40c505b5" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="53628875" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Kundu et al., 2011</paper> <paper entityId="paper-f717d335b5fc0e468f31492d359a2c3a30f614ee" annotationId="ann_013" corpusId="6177564" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Zhang et al., 2014</paper>

paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880ce.displayLabel: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.

s2Metadata.title: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.
s2Metadata.abstract: The ability to precisely control the thermal conductivity (kappa) of a material is fundamental in the development of on-chip heat management or energy conversion applications. Nanostructuring permits a marked reduction of kappa of single-crystalline materials, as recently demonstrated for silicon nanowires. However, silicon-based nanostructured materials with extremely low kappa are not limited to nanowires. By engineering a set of individual phonon-scattering nanodot barriers we have accurately tailored the thermal conductivity of a single-crystalline SiGe material in spatially defined regions as short as approximately 15 nm. Single-barrier thermal resistances between 2 and 4 x 10(-9) m(2) K W(-1) were attained, resulting in a room-temperature kappa down to about 0.9 W m(-1) K(-1), in multilayered structures with as little as five barriers. Such low thermal conductivity is compatible with a totally diffuse mismatch model for the barriers, and it is well below the amorphous limit. The results are in agreement with atomistic Green's function simulations.

paper-965a7f2bf9c14cba930b172313c764df40.displayLabel: Role of light and heavy embedded nanoparticles on the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloys

s2Metadata.title: Role of light and heavy embedded nanoparticles on the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: We have used an atomistic {\it ab initio} approach with no adjustable parameters to compute the lattice thermal conductivity of Si$_{0.5}$Ge$_{0.5}$ with a low concentration of embedded Si or Ge nanoparticles of diameters up to 4.4 nm. Through exact Green's function calculation of the nanoparticle scattering rates, we find that embedding Ge nanoparticles in $\text{Si}_{0.5}\text{Ge}_{0.5}$ provides 20% lower thermal conductivities than embedding Si nanoparticles. This contrasts with the Born approximation which predicts an equal amount of reduction for the two cases, irrespective of the sign of the mass difference. Despite these differences, we find that the Born approximation still performs remarkably well, and it permits investigation of larger nanoparticle sizes, up to 60 nm in diameter, not feasible with the exact approach.

paper-4e8dff46ba90e16bec4eddadf2414abfa3.displayLabel: Unifying first-principles theoretical predictions and experimental measurements of size effects in thermal transport in SiGe alloys

s2Metadata.title: Unifying first-principles theoretical predictions and experimental measurements of size effects in thermal transport in SiGe alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate the correspondence between first principle calculations and experimental measurements of size effects on thermal transport in SiGe alloys. Transient thermal grating (TTG) is used to measure the effective thermal conductivity. The virtual crystal approximation under the density functional theory (DFT) framework combined with impurity scattering is used to determine the phonon properties for the exact alloy composition of the measured samples. With these properties, classical size effects are calculated for the experimental geometry of reflection mode TTG using the recently-developed variational solution to the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE), which is verified against established Monte Carlo simulations. We find agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements in the reduction of thermal conductivity (as much as $\sim$ 25\% of the bulk value) across grating periods spanning one order of magnitude. This work provides a framework for the tabletop study of size effects on thermal transport.

paper-819408632f51db9848aa8f2b19705eeff4.displayLabel: Diameter dependence of SiGe nanowire thermal conductivity

s2Metadata.title: Diameter dependence of SiGe nanowire thermal conductivity
s2Metadata.abstract: We theoretically compute the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloy nanowires as a function of nanowire diameter, alloy concentration, and temperature, obtaining a satisfactory quantitative agreement with experimental results. Our results account for the weaker diameter dependence of the thermal conductivity recently observed in Si$_{1-x}$Ge$_x$ nanowires ($x<0.1$), as compared to pure Si nanowires. We also present calculations in the full range of alloy concentrations, $0 \leq x \leq 1$, which may serve as a basis for comparison with future experiments on high alloy concentration nanowires.

paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6.displayLabel: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art

s2Metadata.title: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art
s2Metadata.abstract: In our environment, the large availability of wasted heat has motivated the search for methods to harvest heat. As a reliable way to supply energy, SiGe has been used for thermoelectric generators (TEGs) in space missions for decades. Recently, micro-thermoelectric generators (μTEG) have been shown to be a promising way to supply energy for the Internet of Things (IoT) by using daily waste heat. Combining the predominant CMOS compatibility with high electric conductivity and low thermal conductivity performance, Si nanowire and SiGe nanowire have been a candidate for μTEG. This review gives a comprehensive introduction of the Si, SiGe nanowires, and their possibility for μTEG. The basic thermoelectric principles, materials, structures, fabrication, measurements, and applications are discussed in depth.

content.title: Mass-only disorder models systematically miss force-constant/strain scattering and bias kappa comparisons

content.text: If you model Ge only by changing its mass, you miss other important scattering mechanisms and can get biased thermal conductivity values and trends.
**Supporting evidence:**

- AGF study of SiGe barriers uses Tersoff for Si but treats Ge in the mass-difference approximation (mass disorder only), and explicitly notes limitations from this approximation and from Tersoff dispersion inaccuracies.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- First-principles nanoparticle study in Si0.5Ge0.5 treats mass-difference as dominant but explicitly discusses that force-constant differences and strain were neglected and estimated as smaller; it also reports computed alloy kappa ~30% higher than experiment, indicating sensitivity to omitted scattering channels and/or approximations (e.g., VCA).  <paper entityId="paper-965a7f2bf9c14cba930b172313c764df40c505b5" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="53628875" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Kundu et al., 2011</paper>

- DFT-BTE + TTG study uses VCA plus impurity scattering and emphasizes that fully spectral solutions are needed; it highlights that simplified heuristics fail, underscoring model-form dependence of inferred kappa suppression when mechanisms are omitted or simplified.  <paper entityId="paper-4e8dff46ba90e16bec4eddadf2414abfa3ca51e7" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="96453663" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Huberman et al., 2017</paper>

content.title: When alloying shifts heat to long-MFP modes, geometry/size effects become more influential and require spectral treatment

content.text: Alloying can make long-traveling phonons matter more, so size and geometry matter more, and you need spectral (not gray) models to predict the result.
**Supporting evidence:**

- TTG + DFT-BTE study of Si0.934Ge0.066 explains that alloy scattering suppresses high-frequency phonons and shifts dominance to longer-MFP modes, leading to strong grating-period dependence and failure of simple MFP-cutoff/gray heuristics; spectral solutions are required.  <paper entityId="paper-4e8dff46ba90e16bec4eddadf2414abfa3ca51e7" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="96453663" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Huberman et al., 2017</paper>

- SiGe nanowire transport theory/review states alloy scattering suppresses high-frequency modes and leads to stronger length dependence and weaker diameter/roughness dependence compared to pure Si, consistent with dominance of low-frequency long-MFP carriers and the need for proper spectral/size treatment.  <paper entityId="paper-819408632f51db9848aa8f2b19705eeff47ff7e1" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="118592133" artifactId="extraction-result-1#uuid-e1.0">Wang et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.5">Li et al., 2021</paper>

- For the same SiGe nanostructure, an AGF or MD model that uses a mass-difference approximation (or otherwise suppresses chemistry-dependent force constants) will predict weaker sensitivity to stiffness-contrast features (e.g., SiC-like stiff inclusions) than a model that includes chemistry-dependent bonding, even if both predict similar trends for purely mass-contrast features.
- Fitted low-order empirical laws for kappa(x,T) derived from finite-size MD boxes will show composition-dependent breakdown near end members more readily than DFT-BTE/VCA curves, because finite-size and potential-dispersion errors are amplified when intrinsic scattering is weak (near pure Si or pure Ge).
- In lightly alloyed SiGe films, spectral BTE models will predict stronger dependence on characteristic experimental length scales (TTG period, film thickness) than gray models, whereas at high alloy fractions (near minimum kappa region) the difference between spectral and gray predictions will shrink.

- A machine-learned potential trained on diverse Si/Ge/C configurations could reconcile both correct dispersion/anharmonicity and correct defect energetics, yielding kappa predictions that match DFT-BTE for bulk while also matching MD for complex nanostructures; whether current foundation models achieve this for SiGeC without retraining is uncertain.
- Cross-method calibration might reveal that some apparent 'sub-alloy-limit' kappa reports in certain geometries are partially attributable to model-form omissions or boundary-condition artifacts, not only to physical spectral coverage; disentangling would require matched phonon spectra and transmission calculations across methods.

- If a mass-only approximation model reproduces experimentally observed stiffness-contrast trends (e.g., stiff inclusions outperforming mass-only predictions) without tuning, then the claim that force-constant/strain omission biases those comparisons is weakened.
- If spectral and gray models agree quantitatively across TTG periods or nanowire lengths even in lightly alloyed SiGe where long-MFP modes should matter, then the asserted necessity of spectral treatment is challenged.
- No direct evidence in the provided dataset links a specific machine-learned potential to kappa predictions for SiGeC; thus, quantitative claims about ML potentials remain untested here.

paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db2.displayLabel: Compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivity below the thin-film alloy limit

s2Metadata.title: Compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivity below the thin-film alloy limit
s2Metadata.abstract: We describe epitaxial Ge/Si multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivities which can be systematically reduced to exceptionally low values, as compared both with bulk and thin-film SiGe alloys of the same average concentration, by simply changing the thicknesses of the constituent layers. Ab initio calculations reveal that partial interdiffusion of Ge into the Si spacers, which naturally results from Ge segregation during growth, plays a determinant role, lowering the thermal conductivity below what could be achieved without interdiffusion (perfect superlattice), or with total interdiffusion (alloy limit). This phenomenon is similar to the one previously observed in alloys with embedded nanoparticles, and it stresses the importance of combining alloy and nanosized scatterers simultaneously to minimize thermal conductivity. Our calculations thus suggest that superlattices with sharp interfaces, which are commonly sought but difficult to realize, are worse than compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers in the search for materials with ultralow thermal conductivities.

paper-f717d335b5fc0e468f31492d359a2c3a30.displayLabel: The best nanoparticle size distribution for minimum thermal conductivity

s2Metadata.title: The best nanoparticle size distribution for minimum thermal conductivity
s2Metadata.abstract: Which sizes of nanoparticles embedded in a crystalline solid yield the lowest thermal conductivity? Nanoparticles have long been demonstrated to reduce the thermal conductivity of crystals by scattering phonons, but most previous works assumed the nanoparticles to have a single size. Here, we use optimization methods to show that the best nanoparticle size distribution to scatter the broad thermal phonon spectrum is not a similarly broad distribution but rather several discrete peaks at well-chosen nanoparticle radii. For SiGe, the best size distribution yields a thermal conductivity below that of amorphous silicon. Further, we demonstrate that a simplified distribution yields nearly the same low thermal conductivity and can be readily fabricated. Our work provides important insights into how to manipulate the full spectrum of phonons and will guide the design of more efficient thermoelectric materials.

paper-3b9d56c73fcc42f28b31eab8ade7dd5068.displayLabel: Thermal transport in nanocrystalline Si and SiGe by ab initio based Monte Carlo simulation

s2Metadata.title: Thermal transport in nanocrystalline Si and SiGe by ab initio based Monte Carlo simulation
s2Metadata.abstract: Nanocrystalline thermoelectric materials based on Si have long been of interest because Si is earth-abundant, inexpensive, and non-toxic. However, a poor understanding of phonon grain boundary scattering and its effect on thermal conductivity has impeded efforts to improve the thermoelectric figure of merit. Here, we report an ab-initio based computational study of thermal transport in nanocrystalline Si-based materials using a variance-reduced Monte Carlo method with the full phonon dispersion and intrinsic lifetimes from first-principles as input. By fitting the transmission profile of grain boundaries, we obtain excellent agreement with experimental thermal conductivity of nanocrystalline Si [Wang et al. Nano Letters 11, 2206 (2011)]. Based on these calculations, we examine phonon transport in nanocrystalline SiGe alloys with ab-initio electron-phonon scattering rates. Our calculations show that low energy phonons still transport substantial amounts of heat in these materials, despite scattering by electron-phonon interactions, due to the high transmission of phonons at grain boundaries, and thus improvements in ZT are still possible by disrupting these modes. This work demonstrates the important insights into phonon transport that can be obtained using ab-initio based Monte Carlo simulations in complex nanostructured materials.

paper-e863d30cedd4a89a375383fa31b4fe495e.displayLabel: Effect of Phonon Dispersion on Thermal Conduction Across Si/Ge Interfaces

s2Metadata.title: Effect of Phonon Dispersion on Thermal Conduction Across Si/Ge Interfaces
s2Metadata.abstract: We report finite-volume simulations of the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) for heat conduction across the heterogeneous interfaces in SiGe superlattices. The diffuse mismatch model incorporating phonon dispersion and polarization is implemented over a wide range of Knudsen numbers. The results indicate that the thermal conductivity of a Si/Ge superlattice is much lower than that of the constitutive bulk materials for superlattice periods in the submicron regime. We report results for effective thermal conductivity of various material volume fractions and superlattice periods. Details of the nonequilibrium energy exchange between optical and acoustic phonons that originate from the mismatch of phonon spectra in silicon and germanium are delineated for the first time. Conditions are identified for which this effect can produce significantly more thermal resistance than that due to boundary scattering of phonons. [DOI: 10.1115/1.4004429]

paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03.displayLabel: Mode localization and suppressed heat transport in amorphous alloys

s2Metadata.title: Mode localization and suppressed heat transport in amorphous alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: Glasses usually represent the lower limit for the thermal conductivity of solids, but a fundamental understanding of lattice heat transport in amorphous materials can provide design rules to beat such a limit. Here we investigate the role of mass disorder in glasses by studying amorphous silicon-germanium alloy (a-${\mathrm{Si}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Ge}}_{x}$) over the full range of atomic concentration from $x=0$ to $x=1$, using molecular dynamics and the quasiharmonic Green-Kubo lattice dynamics formalism. We find that the thermal conductivity of a-${\mathrm{Si}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Ge}}_{x}$ as a function of $x$ exhibits a smoother U shape than in crystalline mass-disordered alloys. The main contribution to the initial drop of thermal conductivity at low Ge concentration stems from the localization of otherwise extended modes that make up the lowest 8% of the population by frequency. Contributions from intermediate frequency modes are decreased more gradually with increasing Ge to reach a broad minimum thermal conductivity between concentrations of Ge from $x=0.25$ to 0.75. Modal analysis unravels the correlations among localization, line broadening, and the contribution to thermal transport of modes within different frequency ranges.

content.title: Mass-only disorder models undercount stiffness/chemistry/topology scattering and therefore tend to overpredict κ when those channels matter

content.text: If you only change masses and not bonds/chemistry, you miss scattering and usually predict too-high thermal conductivity—especially for interfaces and SiC-like inclusions.
**Supporting evidence:**

- AGF calculations for SiGe barriers and nanodot barriers use Tersoff for Si but treat Ge via a mass-difference approximation (mass disorder only, no Ge force-constant differences). The paper flags this as an approximation/limitation and notes Tersoff dispersion inaccuracies; nevertheless, nanodot-induced roughness drives κ close to DMM-like diffusive limits compared with flatter barriers.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- In epitaxial Ge nanodot multilayers, experiments show very low cross-plane κ (~0.9 W/mK) and interpret transport as highly diffusive/additive barrier resistance (DMM-like), indicating strong scattering from interface morphology/topography that goes beyond a simple homogeneous alloy mass-disorder picture.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- Compositionally modulated SiGe multilayers achieve κ below thin-film alloy limits; first-principles BTE modeling explains this by combining scattering from a mean mass-density profile M(z) (barrier-like) with local random fluctuations ΔM (alloy-like), i.e., multiple scattering channels across different frequencies are needed to match experiment.  <paper entityId="paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db24d00dd" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="119227704" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Chen et al., 2013</paper>

- First-principles Si0.5Ge0.5 + nanoparticles study models elastic scattering primarily via mass perturbations (alloy disorder and nanoparticles) and neglects IFC/strain contributions after estimating them small; yet it reports computed κ about ~30% higher than experiment, consistent with missing real-structure scattering (and/or missing IFC/topology disorder).  <paper entityId="paper-965a7f2bf9c14cba930b172313c764df40c505b5" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="53628875" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Kundu et al., 2011</paper>

- The ‘best nanoparticle size distribution’ model explicitly assumes mass-difference dominance and neglects IFC differences between Si and SiGe; it still predicts very large κ reductions by combining point defects + nanoparticles + (optional) grain-boundary scattering, underscoring that when additional scattering channels are included (even phenomenologically) κ can drop far below bulk baselines.  <paper entityId="paper-f717d335b5fc0e468f31492d359a2c3a30f614ee" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="6177564" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Zhang et al., 2014</paper>

content.title: Bulk-perfect-crystal DFT-BTE is a baseline upper envelope; microstructure adds a low-frequency filter that depresses κ

content.text: Perfect-crystal calculations give the high end. Real microstructures usually lower κ, and they do so more when grains/interfaces are small enough to block the long-traveling phonons.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Nanocrystalline SiGe (2% Ge) VRMC BTE: bulk SiGe κ ≈ 34.3 W/mK at 300 K; nanocrystalline 550 nm grains κ ≈ 18.8 W/mK; 20 nm grains κ ≈ 4.6 W/mK—demonstrating monotonic κ suppression with decreasing grain size (increased GB density).  <paper entityId="paper-3b9d56c73fcc42f28b31eab8ade7dd5068c86121" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="14166953" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Yang et al., 2017</paper>

- Nanocrystalline Si VRMC BTE: 20 nm grain size yields κ ≈ 8.4 W/mK at 300 K, far below bulk Si values (~155–166 W/mK used as bulk references in other modeling contexts), consistent with strong low-frequency/MFP filtering by GBs.  <paper entityId="paper-3b9d56c73fcc42f28b31eab8ade7dd5068c86121" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="14166953" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.1">Yang et al., 2017</paper> <paper entityId="paper-e863d30cedd4a89a375383fa31b4fe495e3f96a6" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="14254929" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Singh et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-f717d335b5fc0e468f31492d359a2c3a30f614ee" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="6177564" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Zhang et al., 2014</paper>

- Epitaxial Ge nanodot multilayers: cross-plane κ as low as ~0.9 W/mK at room temperature; interpretation is additive, highly diffusive nanodot-layer resistances with ballistic spacers, i.e., dense barriers suppress the long-MFP contribution and push toward a DMM-like limit.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- Compositionally modulated SiGe multilayers: measured cross-plane κ down to ~2.3 W/mK as mean Ge rises (~12%); first-principles BTE explains κ below alloy limits via combined barrier-like and alloy-like scattering across the spectrum (broadband suppression).  <paper entityId="paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db24d00dd" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="119227704" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Chen et al., 2013</paper>

- Single-crystal Si0.934Ge0.066 TTG + DFT-BTE/VCA: parameter-free BTE matches measured effective κ versus grating period, supporting DFT-BTE as a credible ideal-crystal spectral baseline; size (finite length scale) suppresses κ by reducing contributions from long-MFP modes.  <paper entityId="paper-4e8dff46ba90e16bec4eddadf2414abfa3ca51e7" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="96453663" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Huberman et al., 2017</paper>

- If a SiGe nanocomposite contains chemistry-distinct inclusions (e.g., SiC) rather than isomorphous Si/Ge inclusions, then a mass-only inclusion model will systematically underpredict the inclusion’s κ suppression relative to chemistry-aware (DFT/ML) models because stiffness/topology scattering is missing.
- For a fixed SiGe composition, introducing a microstructure length scale ℓ (grain size, barrier spacing, dot-layer period) that is reduced from >1 µm toward tens of nm will monotonically reduce κ until approaching a diffusive limit; the strongest marginal drop will occur when ℓ crosses the modal MFP range dominating κ in the alloy (shifted toward low-frequency modes by alloy scattering).
- If two models match the same experiment without including microstructure, the one using a more approximate potential/form (e.g., empirical potential with known dispersion issues or mass-only disorder) is more likely achieving agreement by error cancellation; adding explicit microstructure scattering to that model will then overshoot the experimental κ reduction.

- A modern foundation ML potential for Si–Ge–C trained on diverse bonding environments will predict a materially different balance between substitutional C and SiC precipitation under strain than older ML/empirical approaches; if it predicts strong SiC driving force, κ will be dominated by precipitate/interface scattering rather than isolated point-defect scattering even at 1 at% C.
- Including strain-altered force constants (beyond mass-density profiles) in first-principles BTE for coherently strained compositionally modulated SiGe multilayers could change κ in either direction depending on whether strain increases anharmonicity more than it reduces spectral mismatch; the sign may flip with period thickness and Ge profile shape.

- Construct two otherwise identical Si/Ge barrier simulations: one mass-only (Ge as mass substitution in Si) and one chemistry-aware (explicit Si–Ge IFC contrast). If κ does not decrease (or increases) when chemistry-aware force constants are included, the claimed upward bias of mass-only models is falsified for that regime.
- Measure or simulate κ_real/κ_bulk,ideal versus grain size for a SiGe composition while independently characterizing GB transmission; if κ does not decrease as grain size is reduced into the dominant MFP range (without a compensating increase in specularity/transmission), the ‘length-scale low-frequency filter’ rule fails.

- Nanowire-specific diameter/roughness scaling laws and the reported plateau-like κ(x) behavior in some NW theories are not explicitly derived here; this theory focuses on model-form/potential bias and microstructure filtering rather than nanowire confinement formalisms.  <paper entityId="paper-819408632f51db9848aa8f2b19705eeff47ff7e1" annotationId="ann_013" corpusId="118592133" artifactId="extraction-result-1#uuid-e1.0">Wang et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_014" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Li et al., 2021</paper>

- Amorphous SiGe shows κ reductions dominated by mode localization and generalized-velocity suppression rather than crystalline mass-scattering pictures; how potential choice biases amorphous κ is only touched on via special cases, not modeled as a separate law here.  <paper entityId="paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03f6a2b6" annotationId="ann_015" corpusId="226975563" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Lundgren et al., 2020</paper>

paper-3b9d56c73fcc42f28b31eab8ade7dd5068.displayLabel: Thermal transport in nanocrystalline Si and SiGe by ab initio based Monte Carlo simulation

s2Metadata.title: Thermal transport in nanocrystalline Si and SiGe by ab initio based Monte Carlo simulation
s2Metadata.abstract: Nanocrystalline thermoelectric materials based on Si have long been of interest because Si is earth-abundant, inexpensive, and non-toxic. However, a poor understanding of phonon grain boundary scattering and its effect on thermal conductivity has impeded efforts to improve the thermoelectric figure of merit. Here, we report an ab-initio based computational study of thermal transport in nanocrystalline Si-based materials using a variance-reduced Monte Carlo method with the full phonon dispersion and intrinsic lifetimes from first-principles as input. By fitting the transmission profile of grain boundaries, we obtain excellent agreement with experimental thermal conductivity of nanocrystalline Si [Wang et al. Nano Letters 11, 2206 (2011)]. Based on these calculations, we examine phonon transport in nanocrystalline SiGe alloys with ab-initio electron-phonon scattering rates. Our calculations show that low energy phonons still transport substantial amounts of heat in these materials, despite scattering by electron-phonon interactions, due to the high transmission of phonons at grain boundaries, and thus improvements in ZT are still possible by disrupting these modes. This work demonstrates the important insights into phonon transport that can be obtained using ab-initio based Monte Carlo simulations in complex nanostructured materials.

paper-819408632f51db9848aa8f2b19705eeff4.displayLabel: Diameter dependence of SiGe nanowire thermal conductivity

s2Metadata.title: Diameter dependence of SiGe nanowire thermal conductivity
s2Metadata.abstract: We theoretically compute the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloy nanowires as a function of nanowire diameter, alloy concentration, and temperature, obtaining a satisfactory quantitative agreement with experimental results. Our results account for the weaker diameter dependence of the thermal conductivity recently observed in Si$_{1-x}$Ge$_x$ nanowires ($x<0.1$), as compared to pure Si nanowires. We also present calculations in the full range of alloy concentrations, $0 \leq x \leq 1$, which may serve as a basis for comparison with future experiments on high alloy concentration nanowires.

paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6.displayLabel: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art

s2Metadata.title: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art
s2Metadata.abstract: In our environment, the large availability of wasted heat has motivated the search for methods to harvest heat. As a reliable way to supply energy, SiGe has been used for thermoelectric generators (TEGs) in space missions for decades. Recently, micro-thermoelectric generators (μTEG) have been shown to be a promising way to supply energy for the Internet of Things (IoT) by using daily waste heat. Combining the predominant CMOS compatibility with high electric conductivity and low thermal conductivity performance, Si nanowire and SiGe nanowire have been a candidate for μTEG. This review gives a comprehensive introduction of the Si, SiGe nanowires, and their possibility for μTEG. The basic thermoelectric principles, materials, structures, fabrication, measurements, and applications are discussed in depth.

paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db2.displayLabel: Compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivity below the thin-film alloy limit

s2Metadata.title: Compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivity below the thin-film alloy limit
s2Metadata.abstract: We describe epitaxial Ge/Si multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivities which can be systematically reduced to exceptionally low values, as compared both with bulk and thin-film SiGe alloys of the same average concentration, by simply changing the thicknesses of the constituent layers. Ab initio calculations reveal that partial interdiffusion of Ge into the Si spacers, which naturally results from Ge segregation during growth, plays a determinant role, lowering the thermal conductivity below what could be achieved without interdiffusion (perfect superlattice), or with total interdiffusion (alloy limit). This phenomenon is similar to the one previously observed in alloys with embedded nanoparticles, and it stresses the importance of combining alloy and nanosized scatterers simultaneously to minimize thermal conductivity. Our calculations thus suggest that superlattices with sharp interfaces, which are commonly sought but difficult to realize, are worse than compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers in the search for materials with ultralow thermal conductivities.

paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880ce.displayLabel: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.

s2Metadata.title: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.
s2Metadata.abstract: The ability to precisely control the thermal conductivity (kappa) of a material is fundamental in the development of on-chip heat management or energy conversion applications. Nanostructuring permits a marked reduction of kappa of single-crystalline materials, as recently demonstrated for silicon nanowires. However, silicon-based nanostructured materials with extremely low kappa are not limited to nanowires. By engineering a set of individual phonon-scattering nanodot barriers we have accurately tailored the thermal conductivity of a single-crystalline SiGe material in spatially defined regions as short as approximately 15 nm. Single-barrier thermal resistances between 2 and 4 x 10(-9) m(2) K W(-1) were attained, resulting in a room-temperature kappa down to about 0.9 W m(-1) K(-1), in multilayered structures with as little as five barriers. Such low thermal conductivity is compatible with a totally diffuse mismatch model for the barriers, and it is well below the amorphous limit. The results are in agreement with atomistic Green's function simulations.

content.title: Alloy scattering shifts dominant heat flow toward low-frequency modes; added interfaces/GBs then become disproportionately effective

content.text: As you alloy Si with Ge, the remaining heat is carried more by low-frequency phonons—so boundaries and interfaces that block those phonons become especially powerful.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Nanocrystalline SiGe (2% Ge): mass-defect scattering plus GB transmission produces large κ reductions with decreasing grain size, indicating remaining heat flow includes long-MFP modes that GBs can suppress.  <paper entityId="paper-3b9d56c73fcc42f28b31eab8ade7dd5068c86121" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="14166953" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Yang et al., 2017</paper>

- Nanocrystalline Si: at 300 K, low-frequency phonons contribute strongly; GB models emphasize transmission near unity at low ω and reduced transmission at higher ω, showing spectral filtering matters.  <paper entityId="paper-3b9d56c73fcc42f28b31eab8ade7dd5068c86121" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="14166953" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.1">Yang et al., 2017</paper>

- SiGe nanowire modeling and reviews state alloy scattering suppresses high-frequency phonons, making low-frequency phonons dominate and causing stronger length dependence but weaker diameter/roughness dependence in alloys than in pure Si.  <paper entityId="paper-819408632f51db9848aa8f2b19705eeff47ff7e1" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="118592133" artifactId="extraction-result-1#uuid-e1.0">Wang et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.5">Li et al., 2021</paper>

- Compositionally modulated SiGe multilayers: combining barrier-like (low-frequency effective) scattering with alloy-like (high-frequency effective) scattering yields κ below both perfect superlattice and homogeneous alloy limits, consistent with complementary spectral targeting.  <paper entityId="paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db24d00dd" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="119227704" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Chen et al., 2013</paper>

- Ge nanodot multilayers achieve κ close to DMM-like limits; nanodot roughness broadens the scattering influence relative to flat barriers, consistent with enhanced suppression of longer-MFP/low-frequency modes.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

content.title: Broadband design rule: combining M(z) barriers with ΔM randomness (or multi-scale inclusions) can undercut homogeneous-alloy κ

content.text: If you mix ‘barrier-like’ structure with ‘alloy-like’ randomness, you can scatter a wider range of phonons and get κ even lower than a plain alloy.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Compositionally modulated multilayers paper explicitly decomposes scattering into mean mass-density profile M(z) (barrier scattering) plus random ΔM (alloy scattering) and reports that combined presence can lower κ below both homogeneous alloy and ideal sharp-interface superlattice limits.  <paper entityId="paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db24d00dd" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="119227704" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Chen et al., 2013</paper>

- Experimental Ge nanodot multilayers show additive barrier resistances and κ near DMM-like limits, consistent with an incoherent/diffusive regime where adding structured barriers reduces κ beyond what flat alloy barriers achieve.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- AGF simulations comparing flat SiGe barriers vs nanodot barriers show nanodot systems yield lower κ and are closer to DMM than flat barriers, supporting that adding mesoscale morphology (a form of M(z) complexity) increases scattering breadth.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- MD on compositionally graded SiGe nanowires reports substantially reduced κ versus abrupt interfaces (review cites ~57% reduction), consistent with broadened scattering from grading + disorder.  <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.7">Li et al., 2021</paper>

- For Si0.8Ge0.2, introducing nanodot/nanoparticle layers (or GBs) will reduce κ more than the same interface density in pure Si because alloying shifts heat carriage toward long-MFP low-frequency modes that interfaces can filter.
- A compositionally graded profile with residual random alloy disorder will yield lower κ than either (i) a fully homogeneous alloy of the same mean x or (ii) a perfectly abrupt, perfectly periodic superlattice of the same mean x, provided interfaces are sufficiently diffuse/incoherent.
- Adding a second length scale (e.g., nanoparticles + grain boundaries) will produce a super-additive reduction relative to adding either alone if the two target different parts of the phonon spectrum.

- In SiGeC, an engineered tri-modal spectrum of scatterers (substitutional C + SiC precipitates + nanoscale GBs) could push κ below amorphous-Si benchmarks while retaining crystallinity, if stiffness-disorder scattering from SiC is as broadband as hypothesized.
- There may exist an optimal correlated arrangement (not random) of graded composition + nanodots that maximizes broadband suppression without invoking coherent interference, potentially outperforming purely random microstructures.

- If a controlled experiment/simulation shows that adding interfaces/barriers to an alloy reduces κ by the same fraction as in pure Si (after matching interface density and roughness), the predicted alloy-amplified marginal effect is false.
- If graded profiles consistently show higher κ than abrupt interfaces at the same mean composition and defect density in the incoherent regime, the broadband-scattering/inequality rule is falsified.

- This theory does not directly address the detailed potential-dependence or endpoint-composition anomalies that can arise in empirical MD fits; it focuses on physical spectral complementarity rather than numerical artifacts.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03.displayLabel: Mode localization and suppressed heat transport in amorphous alloys

s2Metadata.title: Mode localization and suppressed heat transport in amorphous alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: Glasses usually represent the lower limit for the thermal conductivity of solids, but a fundamental understanding of lattice heat transport in amorphous materials can provide design rules to beat such a limit. Here we investigate the role of mass disorder in glasses by studying amorphous silicon-germanium alloy (a-${\mathrm{Si}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Ge}}_{x}$) over the full range of atomic concentration from $x=0$ to $x=1$, using molecular dynamics and the quasiharmonic Green-Kubo lattice dynamics formalism. We find that the thermal conductivity of a-${\mathrm{Si}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Ge}}_{x}$ as a function of $x$ exhibits a smoother U shape than in crystalline mass-disordered alloys. The main contribution to the initial drop of thermal conductivity at low Ge concentration stems from the localization of otherwise extended modes that make up the lowest 8% of the population by frequency. Contributions from intermediate frequency modes are decreased more gradually with increasing Ge to reach a broad minimum thermal conductivity between concentrations of Ge from $x=0.25$ to 0.75. Modal analysis unravels the correlations among localization, line broadening, and the contribution to thermal transport of modes within different frequency ranges.

paper-e863d30cedd4a89a375383fa31b4fe495e.displayLabel: Effect of Phonon Dispersion on Thermal Conduction Across Si/Ge Interfaces

s2Metadata.title: Effect of Phonon Dispersion on Thermal Conduction Across Si/Ge Interfaces
s2Metadata.abstract: We report finite-volume simulations of the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) for heat conduction across the heterogeneous interfaces in SiGe superlattices. The diffuse mismatch model incorporating phonon dispersion and polarization is implemented over a wide range of Knudsen numbers. The results indicate that the thermal conductivity of a Si/Ge superlattice is much lower than that of the constitutive bulk materials for superlattice periods in the submicron regime. We report results for effective thermal conductivity of various material volume fractions and superlattice periods. Details of the nonequilibrium energy exchange between optical and acoustic phonons that originate from the mismatch of phonon spectra in silicon and germanium are delineated for the first time. Conditions are identified for which this effect can produce significantly more thermal resistance than that due to boundary scattering of phonons. [DOI: 10.1115/1.4004429]

paper-965a7f2bf9c14cba930b172313c764df40.displayLabel: Role of light and heavy embedded nanoparticles on the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloys

s2Metadata.title: Role of light and heavy embedded nanoparticles on the thermal conductivity of SiGe alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: We have used an atomistic {\it ab initio} approach with no adjustable parameters to compute the lattice thermal conductivity of Si$_{0.5}$Ge$_{0.5}$ with a low concentration of embedded Si or Ge nanoparticles of diameters up to 4.4 nm. Through exact Green's function calculation of the nanoparticle scattering rates, we find that embedding Ge nanoparticles in $\text{Si}_{0.5}\text{Ge}_{0.5}$ provides 20% lower thermal conductivities than embedding Si nanoparticles. This contrasts with the Born approximation which predicts an equal amount of reduction for the two cases, irrespective of the sign of the mass difference. Despite these differences, we find that the Born approximation still performs remarkably well, and it permits investigation of larger nanoparticle sizes, up to 60 nm in diameter, not feasible with the exact approach.

paper-f717d335b5fc0e468f31492d359a2c3a30.displayLabel: The best nanoparticle size distribution for minimum thermal conductivity

s2Metadata.title: The best nanoparticle size distribution for minimum thermal conductivity
s2Metadata.abstract: Which sizes of nanoparticles embedded in a crystalline solid yield the lowest thermal conductivity? Nanoparticles have long been demonstrated to reduce the thermal conductivity of crystals by scattering phonons, but most previous works assumed the nanoparticles to have a single size. Here, we use optimization methods to show that the best nanoparticle size distribution to scatter the broad thermal phonon spectrum is not a similarly broad distribution but rather several discrete peaks at well-chosen nanoparticle radii. For SiGe, the best size distribution yields a thermal conductivity below that of amorphous silicon. Further, we demonstrate that a simplified distribution yields nearly the same low thermal conductivity and can be readily fabricated. Our work provides important insights into how to manipulate the full spectrum of phonons and will guide the design of more efficient thermoelectric materials.

paper-4e8dff46ba90e16bec4eddadf2414abfa3.displayLabel: Unifying first-principles theoretical predictions and experimental measurements of size effects in thermal transport in SiGe alloys

s2Metadata.title: Unifying first-principles theoretical predictions and experimental measurements of size effects in thermal transport in SiGe alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate the correspondence between first principle calculations and experimental measurements of size effects on thermal transport in SiGe alloys. Transient thermal grating (TTG) is used to measure the effective thermal conductivity. The virtual crystal approximation under the density functional theory (DFT) framework combined with impurity scattering is used to determine the phonon properties for the exact alloy composition of the measured samples. With these properties, classical size effects are calculated for the experimental geometry of reflection mode TTG using the recently-developed variational solution to the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE), which is verified against established Monte Carlo simulations. We find agreement between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements in the reduction of thermal conductivity (as much as $\sim$ 25\% of the bulk value) across grating periods spanning one order of magnitude. This work provides a framework for the tabletop study of size effects on thermal transport.

content.title: Early-drop law: low-x Ge suppresses low-frequency heat-carrying modes in a-Si

content.text: Adding a few percent Ge to amorphous Si knocks out the most important low-frequency heat carriers first; later Ge additions reduce heat flow more slowly and via broader-band damping.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Room-temperature amorphous SiGe: a-Si κ ≈ 2.2 W/mK; 5% Ge reduces κ by ~0.6 W/mK (to ~1.6 W/mK) and 15% Ge reduces it by an additional ~0.55 W/mK (to ~1.05 W/mK), implying a steep initial drop then diminishing returns at higher x.  <paper entityId="paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03f6a2b6" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="226975563" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Lundgren et al., 2020</paper>

- Mode-resolved contribution: in a-Si the lowest ~8% of modes (0–4 THz in a-Si) contribute ~half of κ; these low-frequency contributions are the ones most strongly suppressed by small Ge concentrations.  <paper entityId="paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03f6a2b6" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="226975563" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Lundgren et al., 2020</paper>

- Mechanism attribution at low x: κ reduction at low x is reported to be dominated by localization and reduced generalized velocities/spatial overlap rather than a large reduction in lifetimes (i.e., not primarily a crystalline-like mass-scattering-MFP picture).  <paper entityId="paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03f6a2b6" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="226975563" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Lundgren et al., 2020</paper>

- Mechanism attribution at higher x: at higher Ge concentrations, spectral broadening (linewidth increase) reduces resonant transport and mode diffusivity; high-frequency localization contributes little to total κ due to small heat-carrying weight.  <paper entityId="paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03f6a2b6" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="226975563" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Lundgren et al., 2020</paper>

content.title: Low-frequency convergence law: finite-size dependence in amorphous κ is dominated by the lowest-frequency sector

content.text: If an amorphous SiGe simulation box is too small, the missing piece is mainly the lowest-frequency heat transport, so κ looks size-dependent for that reason.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Finite-size effects reported: low-frequency modal contributions (<4 THz in a-Si) show the largest finite-size sensitivity; 1728-atom models differ from converged 13824-atom results mostly in the <4 THz region.  <paper entityId="paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03f6a2b6" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="226975563" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Lundgren et al., 2020</paper>

- Convergence statement: small cells are adequate for qualitative trends but underconverged for low-frequency quantitative contributions, indicating that κ size dependence is a low-frequency convergence issue.  <paper entityId="paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03f6a2b6" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="226975563" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Lundgren et al., 2020</paper>

- Reverse-NEMD (or EMD) κ for amorphous Si0.5Ge0.5 will show substantially weaker length dependence than crystalline Si0.5Ge0.5 in comparable cell geometries; any residual length dependence should primarily appear as κ increasing with length as the low-frequency sector becomes better represented.
- For amorphous Si1-xGex near 300 K, κ(x) will be locally concave upward near x=0 (steep initial drop then diminishing returns), and the composition at which the slope noticeably flattens will correlate with when the lowest-frequency sector’s contribution has already been strongly suppressed.

- Introducing nanometer-scale stiff inclusions (e.g., SiC) into amorphous SiGe could either increase κ (if inclusions create percolating extended vibrational pathways) or decrease κ (if interfaces create additional localization/broadening); the sign should depend on inclusion connectivity and interface bonding strength.
- If an ML potential reproduces the amorphous vibrational spectrum more accurately than Tersoff (especially low-frequency modes), it may shift the predicted crossover composition between localization-dominated and broadening-dominated regimes, changing κ(x) curvature while preserving the qualitative early-drop behavior.

- If mode-resolved analysis in amorphous SiGe shows that the lowest-frequency modes remain similarly extended and retain their generalized velocities up to ~10–15% Ge while κ still drops sharply, then localization/reduced generalized-velocity suppression is not the dominant low-x mechanism and the theory fails.
- If κ computed in amorphous SiGe decreases systematically with increasing simulation cell size after robust statistical convergence (contrary to the claim that missing low-frequency contributions are added with size), the finite-size law is wrong or incomplete.
- If κ(x) in amorphous SiGe is found to be nearly linear in x over 0–20% Ge (no strong early drop), the proposed two-regime compositional mechanism is undermined.

- All crystalline SiGe phenomena in the evidence set (e.g., nanodot barriers, planar superlattices, nanocrystalline grain-boundary transmission, nanoparticle scattering in crystals) are outside this theory’s scope, which is limited to fully amorphous networks.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Pernot et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db24d00dd" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="119227704" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Chen et al., 2013</paper> <paper entityId="paper-e863d30cedd4a89a375383fa31b4fe495e3f96a6" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="14254929" artifactId="extraction-result-3#uuid-e3.0">Singh et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-3b9d56c73fcc42f28b31eab8ade7dd5068c86121" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="14166953" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Yang et al., 2017</paper> <paper entityId="paper-965a7f2bf9c14cba930b172313c764df40c505b5" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="53628875" artifactId="extraction-result-5#uuid-e5.0">Kundu et al., 2011</paper> <paper entityId="paper-f717d335b5fc0e468f31492d359a2c3a30f614ee" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="6177564" artifactId="extraction-result-2#uuid-e2.0">Zhang et al., 2014</paper> <paper entityId="paper-4e8dff46ba90e16bec4eddadf2414abfa3ca51e7" annotationId="ann_013" corpusId="96453663" artifactId="extraction-result-6#uuid-e6.0">Huberman et al., 2017</paper> <paper entityId="paper-819408632f51db9848aa8f2b19705eeff47ff7e1" annotationId="ann_014" corpusId="118592133" artifactId="extraction-result-1#uuid-e1.0">Wang et al., 2010</paper> <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_015" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Li et al., 2021</paper>
