paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880ce.displayLabel: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.

s2Metadata.title: Precise control of thermal conductivity at the nanoscale through individual phonon-scattering barriers.
s2Metadata.abstract: The ability to precisely control the thermal conductivity (kappa) of a material is fundamental in the development of on-chip heat management or energy conversion applications. Nanostructuring permits a marked reduction of kappa of single-crystalline materials, as recently demonstrated for silicon nanowires. However, silicon-based nanostructured materials with extremely low kappa are not limited to nanowires. By engineering a set of individual phonon-scattering nanodot barriers we have accurately tailored the thermal conductivity of a single-crystalline SiGe material in spatially defined regions as short as approximately 15 nm. Single-barrier thermal resistances between 2 and 4 x 10(-9) m(2) K W(-1) were attained, resulting in a room-temperature kappa down to about 0.9 W m(-1) K(-1), in multilayered structures with as little as five barriers. Such low thermal conductivity is compatible with a totally diffuse mismatch model for the barriers, and it is well below the amorphous limit. The results are in agreement with atomistic Green's function simulations.

paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db2.displayLabel: Compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivity below the thin-film alloy limit

s2Metadata.title: Compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivity below the thin-film alloy limit
s2Metadata.abstract: We describe epitaxial Ge/Si multilayers with cross-plane thermal conductivities which can be systematically reduced to exceptionally low values, as compared both with bulk and thin-film SiGe alloys of the same average concentration, by simply changing the thicknesses of the constituent layers. Ab initio calculations reveal that partial interdiffusion of Ge into the Si spacers, which naturally results from Ge segregation during growth, plays a determinant role, lowering the thermal conductivity below what could be achieved without interdiffusion (perfect superlattice), or with total interdiffusion (alloy limit). This phenomenon is similar to the one previously observed in alloys with embedded nanoparticles, and it stresses the importance of combining alloy and nanosized scatterers simultaneously to minimize thermal conductivity. Our calculations thus suggest that superlattices with sharp interfaces, which are commonly sought but difficult to realize, are worse than compositionally-modulated Si1-xGex multilayers in the search for materials with ultralow thermal conductivities.

paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6.displayLabel: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art

s2Metadata.title: Si and SiGe Nanowire for Micro-Thermoelectric Generator: A Review of the Current State of the Art
s2Metadata.abstract: In our environment, the large availability of wasted heat has motivated the search for methods to harvest heat. As a reliable way to supply energy, SiGe has been used for thermoelectric generators (TEGs) in space missions for decades. Recently, micro-thermoelectric generators (μTEG) have been shown to be a promising way to supply energy for the Internet of Things (IoT) by using daily waste heat. Combining the predominant CMOS compatibility with high electric conductivity and low thermal conductivity performance, Si nanowire and SiGe nanowire have been a candidate for μTEG. This review gives a comprehensive introduction of the Si, SiGe nanowires, and their possibility for μTEG. The basic thermoelectric principles, materials, structures, fabrication, measurements, and applications are discussed in depth.

paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03.displayLabel: Mode localization and suppressed heat transport in amorphous alloys

s2Metadata.title: Mode localization and suppressed heat transport in amorphous alloys
s2Metadata.abstract: Glasses usually represent the lower limit for the thermal conductivity of solids, but a fundamental understanding of lattice heat transport in amorphous materials can provide design rules to beat such a limit. Here we investigate the role of mass disorder in glasses by studying amorphous silicon-germanium alloy (a-${\mathrm{Si}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Ge}}_{x}$) over the full range of atomic concentration from $x=0$ to $x=1$, using molecular dynamics and the quasiharmonic Green-Kubo lattice dynamics formalism. We find that the thermal conductivity of a-${\mathrm{Si}}_{1\ensuremath{-}x}{\mathrm{Ge}}_{x}$ as a function of $x$ exhibits a smoother U shape than in crystalline mass-disordered alloys. The main contribution to the initial drop of thermal conductivity at low Ge concentration stems from the localization of otherwise extended modes that make up the lowest 8% of the population by frequency. Contributions from intermediate frequency modes are decreased more gradually with increasing Ge to reach a broad minimum thermal conductivity between concentrations of Ge from $x=0.25$ to 0.75. Modal analysis unravels the correlations among localization, line broadening, and the contribution to thermal transport of modes within different frequency ranges.

content.title: Independent-resistor additivity for highly diffusive nanodot barriers

content.text: If each nanodot layer scatters diffusively, adding more layers adds resistance almost linearly, so thermal conductivity drops as the barrier layers get denser—until spacer resistance or saturation limits further drops.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Experiments on epitaxial Si with vertically stacked Ge nanodot layers report that transport is ballistic in Si spacers (due to long phonon MFPs) while scattering is dominated by independent nanodot layers, so total resistance is interpreted as the sum of barrier resistances; measured κ_cross-plane reaches (0.9 ± 0.1) W/m-K for a ~15.5 nm region with 5 nanodot layers and ~3.7 nm period, and per-barrier resistances are discussed as additive and DMM-like.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- AGF simulations of nanodot-barrier multilayers yield conductivities close to the DMM limit and in reasonable agreement with experiment, supporting the assumption that each nanodot barrier behaves as a highly diffusive scatterer whose resistance can be treated in an incoherent/additive manner at the device scale (within modeling approximations).  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

content.title: Nanodot morphology enhances low-frequency scattering relative to flat disordered alloy barriers

content.text: Nanodots scatter long-wavelength phonons better than flat alloy layers, so they reduce thermal conductivity more and push behavior toward a diffuse-interface limit.
**Supporting evidence:**

- AGF calculations explicitly comparing flat Si0.5Ge0.5 barriers to lens-shaped nanodot barriers show the nanodot systems yield significantly lower κ and are close to DMM and experiments, while flat barriers yield higher κ. The mechanism attributed is that nanodots introduce larger-scale roughness features that reduce low-frequency phonon mean free paths relative to flat disordered interfaces; high-frequency behavior is more similar between flat and nanodot cases.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- Experiments on epitaxial Ge nanodot multilayers in Si report very low κ_cross-plane (down to ~0.9 W/m-K) and interpret the nanodot layers as highly diffusive barriers consistent with DMM-like limits; the paper contrasts this with prior flat-barrier superlattice literature that exhibits higher κ/less diffusive behavior.  <paper entityId="paper-22fabf3e6c9a3c31c939875049b07880cee85122" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="5410713" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Pernot et al., 2010</paper>

- Compositionally modulated SiGe multilayers (graded/interdiffused planar profiles) are predicted and measured to achieve κ lower than abrupt-barrier or homogeneous-alloy limits because combining barrier-like scattering (effective at low frequencies) with alloy disorder (effective at high frequencies) broadens the scattered frequency range. This supports the broader principle that adding structural nonuniformity that targets low-frequency phonons can outperform purely planar composition disorder alone.  <paper entityId="paper-54a4236f67a2c9f7f1885ceb2eeeda5db24d00dd" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="119227704" artifactId="extraction-result-4#uuid-e4.0">Chen et al., 2013</paper>

- Keeping total Ge volume fraction fixed (<~20%) in an epitaxial Si matrix, converting planar SiGe barrier layers into nanodot (3D topographic) barrier layers will reduce κ_cross-plane and move the measured per-barrier resistance closer to full-dispersion DMM estimates; the effect will be strongest at room temperature where long-MFP acoustic modes contribute substantially.
- At fixed dot morphology and similar dot size distribution, κ_cross-plane will approximately follow R_tot ≈ N·R_barrier + R_spacers: doubling the number of nanodot layers (at similar spacers) will increase total resistance approximately linearly until spacer resistance becomes non-negligible.
- If dot morphology is progressively smoothed (e.g., annealing that rounds features and reduces height variation without changing average Ge content much), κ_cross-plane will increase toward the planar-barrier trend, with the largest relative recovery in contributions from low-frequency modes.

- If nanodot barrier layers are partially amorphized (confined to dot regions) while spacers remain crystalline, per-barrier resistance may increase beyond the DMM-like crystalline-interface limit by adding localized vibrational states; whether κ decreases further or saturates depends on whether the current nanodot layers are already near the maximum diffusive scattering attainable for the dominant low-frequency modes.
- Applying coherent biaxial strain to the Si spacer regions (without introducing dislocations) could either increase or decrease R_barrier depending on how strain shifts acoustic mismatch and mode conversion at the dot/spacer interface; a sign change with temperature is possible if different spectral regions dominate at different T.

- Measure κ_cross-plane for otherwise identical multilayers while varying only the number of nanodot layers N at fixed total thickness (compensating spacer thickness accordingly). If R_tot is not approximately linear in N in the regime where barriers are claimed to be independent, the additivity assumption is falsified.
- Create a planar-barrier multilayer engineered to have similar roughness amplitude/correlation lengths as the nanodot case (e.g., intentionally roughened planar interfaces). If κ matches the nanodot case, then nanodot-specific morphology is not the controlling factor; if κ remains higher, it supports the unique low-frequency scattering role of true 3D topography.
- Perform spectral/size-sensitive measurements (e.g., varying spacer thickness systematically) to see whether the inferred per-barrier resistance is constant. Strong spacer-thickness dependence of extracted R_barrier would indicate non-independent barriers or coherent effects.

- The theory does not address substitutional carbon in SiGe, SiC nanoinclusions, or carbon-driven local chemical ordering (Si-rich shells), which are central to other hypotheses in the mission statement but absent from the nanodot evidence base here.  <paper entityId="paper-205cfdd7bb8ec9b05cde1fa02de16869d6ac8e12" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="232358380" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.10">Li et al., 2021</paper>

- The theory does not attempt to explain amorphous SiGe thermal conductivity trends or localization physics in glasses, which involve different mechanisms than interface/barrier-dominated crystalline multilayers.  <paper entityId="paper-35ae656974b99801eb74280f0e580f0e03f6a2b6" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="226975563" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Lundgren et al., 2020</paper>
